GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

JOSEPH LIEB SHELL
GRAND MASTER

JOEL. SHELL
Grand Master
October 2, 1959 ~September 30, 1960

Joseph Lieb Shell, Grand Master in California for the term ending
September 30, 1960, has devoted his full time during his term of office
to the affairs of the Grand Lodge, having retired from the bench of the
Superior Court of California, in and for the County of San Diego, on
January 6, 1960.
He was born on February 18, 1892, a few miles from Chapman,
Kansas. His parents were Charles Ellsworth Shell and Ida A. Robinson
Shell. His father, an alumnus of Otterbein College in Westerville,
Ohio, was a rural school teacher, and became the first Principal of the
Dickinson County High School. In 1895 he entered the United States
Indian Service and was assigned to the Rosebud Indian Reservation
in South Dakota.
After some years of service there, the family was transferred to a
school near Greenville, California. Charles Shell became a Mason, and,
after serving as Junior Warden of Sincerity Lodge No. 132, was
elected Senior Warden but was again transferred and unable to serve
as such. The transfer, in 1905, was to the Pala Indian Agency in San
Diego County. In the meantime, our future Grand Master, together
with his two older brothers, was for two years a cadet at the Los
Angeles Military Academy, situated in the vicinity of First and Com~
monwealth Streets in Los Angeles.
When the family moved to San Diego County, the three boys
enrolled at San Diego High School, but another transfer took them to
the Cheyenne and Arapahoe Agency near El Reno, Oklahoma. There
Joe attended high school for three years, graduating from El- Reno
High School in 1909, and in the fall of 1909 enrolled at the University
of Colorado at Boulder. During his first college year he was tackle on
the freshman football team.
When the family was transferred to Kingman, Arizona, Joe enrolled
at the University of California at Berkeley, graduating therefrom in
1913 with the degree of Bachelor of Arts.
After working on surveying projects for six months he entered
the School of Law at the University of California and pursued his legal
studies there for one semester. Lack of finances resulted in his return
to employment at surveying.
His marriage to Nell Schunemann, an Escondido girl, on February
18, 1915, was the beginning of a long and happy life together. Shortly
the Shells, on Joe's entry into the Indian Service, went to La Conner,
Washington. It was there that their two children, Cheryl Ann and
Joseph C., were born, and it was there that Joe received the degrees
of Masonry in Garfield Lodge No. 41. He was initiated on October 26,
1918, passed November 23, 1918, and raised January 24, 1919. It is
interesting to note the coincidence that his son, Joe, received his Masonic

degrees in James A. Garfield Lodge No. 566. in Los Angeles, in September, 1958. The daughter is a Past Matron of San Diego Chapter No.
264, Order of the Eastern Star, of which Chapter Mrs. Shell is also a
member.
Believing that his ambition to be admitted to the practice of law
would be furthered thereby, Joe resigned from the Indian Service and
returned to San Diego, where he was soon employed as Deputy County
Probation Officer and then as Deputy County Clerk, where he was
in constant contact with the Courts while pursuing his study of law.
He was successful at the 1922 summer bar examination and was admitted to practice law in September, 1922. He was soon thereafter
appointed City Prosecutor of the City of San Diego and, after a year
and a half 1n that office, became Deputy District Attorney for the
County of San Diego. leaving that office after two years. He then
engaged in the private practice of law for eight years.
In 1934, with the endorsement of the Bar Association of San Diego,
he ran for, and was elected to the office of Justice of the Peace of San
Diego Township. This court shortly thereafter became the Municipal
Court of the City of San Diego. He served in that court until January.
1945, when , having been elected Judge of the Superior Court, he assumed that office, was re-elected without opposition in 1950 and in
1956. The latter election was for the term which would have ended in
January, 1963, but for his retirement on January 6, 1960.
On April 2, 1926, he affiliated with San Diego Lodge No. 35, served
as Junior Steward in 1926, Senior Steward in 1927, Junior Deacon in
1928, Senior Deacon in 1929, Junior Warden in 1930, Senior Warden
in 1931, and Master in 1932.
He was a member of the Masonic Homes Endowment Board for
eight years, served as Senior Grand Steward of this Grand Lodge in
1940, was a member of the Grand Lodge Committee on Appeals and
Grievances from 1941 to 1956, being Chairman of that Committee during
the last four years of such service. He was elected Junior Grand Warden
in 1956 and has successively served as Senior Grand Warden, Deputy
Grand Master and Grand Master.
He is a member and Past High Priest of San Diego Chapter No.
61, Royal Arch ·Masons, a member of San Diego Council No. 23. Roya l
and Select Masters, San Diego Commandery No. 25, Knights Templar
and the San Diego Scottish Rite Bodies. He was Knighted a K. C. C. H.
in October. 1947, Coroneted an Honorary 33rd Degree Mason in
January, 1956, is a member of Al Bahr Temple, A. A. 0. N. M. S., and
is a Past Soverign of the San Diego Conclave, Red Cross of Constantine.
He is a dual member of Garfield Lodge No. 41, State of Washington,
and of San Diego Lodge No. 35, of California, as well as being a member
of Southern California Research Lodge.
Work with boys has always interested him. He has been for many
years Chairman of the Board of Directors of the Breitbard Athletic

Foundation of San Diego. His interest in youth was strengthened by
his service as Deputy Probation Officer and two years as Judge of the
Juvenile Court of San Diego.
He is also a member of San Diego Chapter No. 264, Order of the
Eastern Star, which he served as Worthy Patron in 1936. His son,
Joseph C., has been for seven years a member of the California State
Assembly and is now Minority Leader in the Assembly.
Joe and Mrs. Shell are proud of their six grandchildren and their
one great-granddaughter.
This man says that he has been most fortunate-because of his
modest success in life, because of his 6ne family, and because o f the
affection which his Brethren have always displayed toward him. H is
hobbies are ·golf, pictures and travel. May his future life be even happier
than it has been in the past. We know his devotion to Masonry will
be continued with the same vigor which has always imbued him.

Great Archite ct of the Universe:
As the celestial bodies move on in their appoint ed
course, and as with the passing of another year the
Grand Lodge of Masons of California convene s for its
deliberations. we ask Thy blessing upon our beloved
Fratern ity and upon all of its officers and member s,
withers oever dispersed.
W e most humbly beseech Thee, of Thy goodne ss, to
comfort and assist all those who are in trouble, sorrow,
need. sickness, or any other adversity. And we ask that
Thou wilt grant to this assemb ly wisdom in all its doings,
strength of mind in all of its difficulties and the beauty of
harmon y in all its underta kings-that its decisions and
selections may be worthy in Thy sight. Amen.

THE POWE R OF FAITH
THE VERY REVEREND ROBERT B. WATTS, D.D .. LL. D.
Grand Chaplain
Most Worshipful Grand Master and Brethre n of the Grand Lodge:
Before proceed ing with the more formal portion of our devotio na l
service, I beg your indulge nce for the express ion of some of the
persona] feelings with which my heart is filled on this occassio n.
First of all, I shall forever be indebte d to the Grand Master for the
opportu nity which he gave me to serve as Grand Chapla in during the
y~ar which has passed so swiftly. Second ly, I cherish very deeply
the
friendsh ip and affection with which my brother officers of the Grand
Lodge have received my efforts. And finally, I thank you, my brethre n of
the Craft. for the rich experie nces and new appreci ation of the depths of
our brother hood which you have revealed to me from one end of
Califor nia to the other, and through the lovely Islands of Hawaii.
Sometim es. I admit, there have been unexpec ted occurre nces-bu t
no clergym an is usually too much surprise d by the unexpec ted. There
have been, for example, such ordinar y vicissitu des as tidal waves,
automo bile wrecks, missed airplane s, gusts of wind sweepin g away
notes during public ceremon ies, flags falling at inoppor tune times, and
heavy concent rations of creamed chicken as the Grand Chaplai n has
accomp lished his appoint ed rounds. Indeed, there have been even more
hilariou s moment s when the Grand Chaplai n has sent charmin g hostesses flying in dismay to their husband s to find out what a Roman
Catholic Priest was doing with a group of Masoni c Grand Lodge
officers.
But as any of my predece ssors will join me in affirming, the wealth of
friendsh ip and the deeper appreci ation of Masonr y which comes from

13

acting as your Grand Chaplai n is a thing for which we are in your debt
forever.
As early in the past Masoni c year as the Sunday following his installatio n, the Grand Master struck a keynote which, to his honor, he
has constan tly develop ed in his talks to the Craft through out the year.
He used, as that keynote . the first of the ancient charges : "You agree to
be a good man and true, and strictly to obey the moral law."
You will see how the develop ment of that injuncti on has served to
prepare the way for my own endeavo rs which I have sought to build
upon the exhorta tion prescrib ed for a newly appoint ed Chaplai n :
"That Holy Book which adorns our sacred altar is the great light
in Masonr y, and forever sheds it benigna nt rays upon every lawful
assemb lage of Free and Accepte d Masons . Teach us from its life-giving
precept s; invoke upon our labors the blessing of that Divine Being whose
infinite goodne ss it so fully reveals and unfolds to us; and guide us by
its lessons of wisdom and truth-. "
So, in great humility . I have sought to do-and so again in this
period of devotio n, in the na me of God the Father of all mankin d. I
invite your attentio n to certain basic and practica l applicat ions of that
·'great light in Masonr y."
In Lord Tennys on's "Idylls of the King," Ambros ius the monk says
of the Knights of the Round Table:
"For good ye are, and bad, and like to coinsSome true, some light, but every one of you
Stampe d with the image of the King."
And so it might be said of us, mixture s as we are of good and bad
but every one of us made in the image of God and possess ed of the
power. if we will but use it. to bring our lives into harmon y with His
immuta ble laws and to enjoy the peace and power which come to us as
we achieve that harmon y. As Master Masons we conceal these truths
in many places in and about the Temple- not the least of which consists
of the teachin gs of our three degrees themse lves-wi th the materia lism
of the First Degreee , and the intellec tualism of the Second Degree
brough t into Divine harmon y and balance by the spiritua l teachin gs of
the Third Degree.
Stated more bluntly . we are in despera te need of some effective
spiritua l power if we are to find the remedy for our modern day tensions, concern s and worries as they assail us on the everyda y levels of
things and thought s.
As I have travelle d about the country , a nd come into contact with
men and women of all ages. and all sorts of backgro unds, if there has
been one common note in the experie nces of all I would unhesit atingly
say that that common note was and is fear.

True indeed is the old French proverb which runs:
"Some of your griefs you have cured,
And the sharpest you still have survived;
But what torments of pain you endured
From evils that never arrived."
Despite this truth, all of us are constantly assailed by fear- which
strikes us from many sides.

1£ we have but the slightest knowledge of the awesome power of
nuclear energy. and if we but scan the largest headlines describing the
incredible weapons now capable of hurling terrestial destruction through
trackless space, we shall know the fear of imminent destruction. Beyond
this, we all too often see and fear in our personal affairs what has been
described in poetic language' as "The black and awful chaos of the
night." We fear the loss of hard-won security, through illness. loss of
jobs. and forces of technology. We fear the loss of friends-and most
of all we fear the unknown, the very essence of mystery and concern.
These fears cripple us. They destroy our minds and bodies, sometimes far beyond repair. Failing this, they darken our lives, subject us
to tensions and make us slaves to our worries. Shakespeare said 2 :
"Our doubts are traitors,
And make us lose the good we oft might win
By fearing to attempt."
What, then, do we find men doing when these gnawing fears attack
them. Do some sturdier or more fortunate ones face their fears squarely
and. by an exercise of their unaided will, successfully command them to
disappear? The answer is "No, not without some further power to aid
them," for no "operation bootstrap" will ever succeed in talking oneself
out of his fears.
Faced with this fact, unhappily we see worried, tense ,and fearful
men and women turning blindly to all sorts of nostrums in their search
for relief and freedom of mind. The crudest attempts of tltis sort lie in
seeking to deaden the mind, with alcohol or narcotics, to the point where,
as I have frequently pointed out, we now see countless lurid advertisements for tranquilizers-including tranquilizers for our pet cats and
dogs. But neither drunkenness nor insensibility touch our fears. Instead ,
they multiply them by constituting in themselves additional valid reasons
for worry and fear.
'Robinson's "Credo."
•"Measure for Measure."

Many of us look for relief from our desperate tensions in the
acquiring of things. We devote ourselves, often with considerable
ruthlessness, to the accumulation of wealth as a means of security and
peace. We think that everything will be solved if we have enough
money. insurance, stocks, bonds, and real estate. But this resort is also
sterile-as witness the total inability of wealth to sustain us in the loss
of health, or the deep sorrows of personal bereavement.
Long ago , our Biblicill great light revealed the uselessness of this
approach in its recital of the experience of the rich man. Here was a man
who had apparently come to within a step of his goal of security. His
crops and material wealth were so huge that he decided to pull down his
old barns and to build huge new ones-in which he would store all his
riches. And then, the Great Light tells us. he said to himself, "Soul. thou
hast much goods laid up for many years; take thine ease, eat. drink and
be merry." But God said to him, "Thou fool. this night thy soul shall be
required of thee; then whose shall those things be which thou hast provided?" And the account speaks straight to us. as well as to the rich
man, when it concludes: "So is he that layeth up treasure for himself.
and is not rich toward God."
Where, then, if these material resources fail us, must we seek for
Man's most-sought prize of freedom from fear? Listen to these revealing
words of Cowper's 8 :
"Ye fearful saints fresh courage take,
The clouds ye so much dread
Are big with mercy. and shall break
In blessings on your head.
Judge not the Lord by feeble sense.
But trust him for his grace;
Behind a frowning Providence
He hides a smiling face."
Here indeed, and not in self-help, lies the road to recovery from
the negative fears of Life which possess us. That road replaces negative
fear by positive faith in some power. outside ourselves. higher than hope
and deeper than fear-a faith which the poet's intuition sees in the
purpose of God for the world.
"Faith is not sig ht, faith is not feeling. nor is it credulity, nor is it
superstition, nor any dodge of bribing God or drugging self, but it is
deep, sure confidence in the character of that God Who has come to the
rescue of the character of Man-.' '•
'"Olney Hymns."
"'The Adventure of Faith," Father Andrew.

It is the kind of mangnificent faith in God, the Supreme Architect
and Ruler of the Universe. which is described in a famous passage of
Paul's letter to the Hebrews:

unworthy, and that anyway as a man accustomed to command he knew
that Jesus needed only to utter a command to accomplish the healing.

"And what shall I more say? for the time would fail me
to tell of Gideon. and of Barak. and of Samson, and of
J eptha; of David also, and Samuel. and of the prophets,
"Who through faith subdued kingdoms, wrought righteousness,
obtained promises, stopped the mouths of lions.
"Quenched the violence of fire. escaped the edge of the
sword, out of weakness were made strong, waxed valiant
in fight, turned to flight the armies of the aliens."
We need an acceptance of belief in that kind of positive action and
power of Almighty God. That's what we mean when we talk about
faith.
And then we need to back up that faith and express our belief in it
by positive action in our lives.
First we must have the faith. And then we must act upon the faith.
Both must go together.
Right here we encounter a great truth which Jesus of Nazareth
revealed to us many times in the recorded instances of the miracles of
healing. Yet it is a truth which frequently never occurs to us as we read
our Bibles.
In instance after instance in the miracles of healing, there was first
an expression of the sick person's faith-cf belief in the supreme healing
power of God. And in every instance of healing, that faith-that belief
-was followed up and expressed by action on the part of the afflicted.
Only then were the healings effected.
Take the instance recited by Matthew concerning the healing of the
woman long ill of an issue of blood. She believed, and then acted on
her belief, that if she could but touch the hem of the Master's garment
she would be healed.
"And Jes us turned him about, and when he saw her, he
said, Daughter, be of good comfort; thy faith hath made
thee whole."
And the woman was instantly healed.
There we have the triple action. First, her complete faith in the
power of God. Second, her action in touching the garment. And third,
the swift response of healing.
Th en there is the thrilling story of the healing of the centurion's
servant. You recall how the centurion came to Jes us and asked him to
heal his sick servant who was at home. Jesus said he would come-but
the centurion told him that that was not necessary- that his house was

Jesus marvelled, we are told, and said to his followers:
"Verily I say unto you, I have not found so great faith,
no, not in Israel.
"And Jesus said unto the centurion, Go thy way, and as
thou hast believed, so be it done unto thee. And his servant
was healed in the self-same hour."
These recorded instances could, of course. be multiplied time and
again from the Scriptures. Always the pattern and the great truth
revealed are the same.
Faith-action in reliance upon that faith- and the power of God
coming in swift response-these are the forces which overcome fear.
Nor are these by any means purely historic events, with no personal
relation to us and to our lives. We too, can have and use just such
faith to defeat our fears of Life if we will only believe and act on our
belief in the power of God to flood our lives and strengthen us with His
limitless power.
Do we say that we lack the power to have such faith? Do we think
that in our particular lives there just isn't that much belief?
That is a fair question-and the answer is direct and crystal clear.
We have an amazing amount of faith, on which we act and ·i ndeed bet
our very lives day after day.
We have faith each day that hundreds of persons unknown to us
will perform tasks which will bring us our food, without which we
would starve.
We have faith in the arbitrary value printed upon pieces of paper-and depend upon money to return th e equivalent of our labor.
We venture upon bridges, elevators, highways--1n tunnels, airplanes, and automobiles-we drink medicines, accept anesthesia and
undergo massive surgery-all in faith of our fellow man.
Faith? We live by faith in unknown men at every turn. We are full
of faith, and what's more, we act and depend upon that faith every day
of our lives.
Are we then a fraid to accept and to act upon a faith in God, the
mighty Creator of the Universe? Time and time again throughout the
ages He has demonstrated His quick response with the flood of His
power-whenever men have tapped that power by faith and by action
in that faith.
Once we realize the availability in our own lives of the power which
springs from our faith, certainly we should, as master builders, promptly
use this knowledge in the designs upon our trestle boards. And let us
be mindful that;

"There is no noble height thou canst not climb;
All tl'iumphs may be thine in Time's futurity,
If. whatsoever thy fault, thou dost not faint or halt;
But lean upon the staff of God's security."
Indeed, wherever we look in our M asonic surroundings, throughout
all the sweep of this Grand Jurisdiction, we see the power of faith in
God in action. And it is a thrilling and heart-warming vista.
This beautiful Memorial Temple in which we meet is itself the
confirmation and reality which crowns the faith of those Past Grand
Officers who had the vision of its possibility and the faith that it could
be achieved-just as it reflects the supporting and creative faith of the
members of the Craft whose imagina tions and outpouring generosity
were activated by that vision of its leaders.
And time after time during the past year. as the officers of this Grand
Lodge have met to lay the cornerstone of. or to dedicate, new Masonic
Temples, they have been deeply moved to see well-planned, wellconstructed and beautiful edifices which-with the devoted physical
labor of the members of a Lodge-have triumphantly come into being
despite what had often appeared hopeless financial limitations. The
brethren had faith, and they acted upon that faith, and through the
power and grace of God they succeeded magnificently.
We have seen the faithful efforts of devoted brothers bring about
priceless results in the lives of young men and young women with
whom they have worked in Masonically sponsored organizations.
These fine young people have been helped to mature, to become responsible members of their group and of their community. and to catch
a vision of unselfishness and of high ideals which will serve them, and
our nation, all their lives.
We have seen-in our Masonic homes-perhaps the purest reflection
of the Divine laws of love and brotherhood. Here indeed is the rare
flower of faith renewed in the hearts and minds of those unable, because
of youth or old-age, to protect and care for themselves. And the great
truth is again revealed to all whose giving has made possible these acts
of brotherhood-that unto him who gives of his substance to relieve the
want of others. there returns a joy and satisfaction a thousand-fold
greater than the gi ft.
We have seen-and perhaps more especially so in the confidences
which are opened to us in our capacity as minister and Grand Chaplain
-faith in God's goodness and power and forgiveness as it has renewed
the courage of the sick and the distressed, as it has strengthened the
dying. and as it has flowed secretly through the handclasp of one brother
reaching out to another in times of stress and adversity.
These are but samples of the product of faith. Others surround us,
if we will but look for them.

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

19

For the priceless truth of the power of God which each one of us
can bring into our personal lives by faith , and action upon that faith,
I commend to your constan t reading "that Holy Book which adorns our
sacred altar." never as a mere ornament, but as "the great light in
Masonry"-ever ready to "guide us by its lessons of wisdom and truth."
Therein are to be found the true secrets of a Master Mason, tha t
knowledge which sets him apart and which permits him, however dark
and fearsome the way, to look up and see "the star-dust, that is whirled
aloft and flies from the invisible chariot wheels of God."

JoE L. SHELL, Grand Master

My Brethren of California and Hawaii:
The term of office of the presently acting elective and appointive
officers of your Grand Lodge is about to expire. In accordance with
custom I shall, without too much detail. make this report to you for your
consideration and, where appropriate, your action.
It has been my privilege to be received formally by districts or Lodges
on 58 occasions. The hospitality and fraternal affection extended everywhere has been outstanding. No one serving as Grand Master could be
mistaken in his belief that our brethren love this fraternity and are proud
of its accomplishments, and that this affection and pride are reflected in
the attachment to. and affection for, those who represent the Grand
Lodge.
In addition to the formal receptions tendered to the Grand Master.
your Grand Lodge officers have on 28 occasions opened the Grand
Lodge in Special Communication for the purpose of Constitution of five
new Lodges, the Dedication of twelve new Masonic Temples, the laying
of flve cornerstones for new public school buildings or new civic buildings, and for one most unusual cornerstone ceremony, that of laying
the cornerstone for a new Church building. The latter ceremony, at the
request of the authorities of the California Heights Methodist Church
in Long Beach, was a most gratifying one by reason of the display of
cordial feeling between our brethren and those of the Church.
In addition to the ceremonies for which Special Communications of
the Grand Lodge were called, we have this year instituted six new
Lodges, some of which, no doubt, will be granted Charters at this Annual Communication, and we have dedicated seven new public school
buildings at the request of school authorities.
We have also been graciously received on sixty-two other occasions.
A detailed report of the activities mentioned is attached hereto as appendant exhibits.
The year has been a busy one. I have no doubt that as time passes by,
the number of appearances by the Grand Master will necessarily increase, as has been true in the past years.
In this respect, I humbly express to the Grand Lodge the opinion
that the affairs of Masonry in this Grand Jurisdiction have grown in
volume and importance to the point where we should begin to think
of relieving our Grand Master of much of the detail attendant upon the
office. I think I may safely say that the Fraternity has, in recent years,
been deprived of the service of several of our outstanding brethren who
are very active in their respective occupations or professions and so not

RESIGNATION OF GRAND LECTURER
During the month of December. 1959, I reluctantly accepted the resignation of the Very Worshipful Elbert W. Davis. who has faithfully
and devotedly given his time and talent to this Grand Lodge as Grand
Lecturer for many years.
The reasons for his submission of his resignation did not seem to me
to be compelling, but to him they seemed so. He is well aware of my
warm regard for him. I feel that this Grand Lodge is deeply indebted
to him for his service to it, and will show its appreciation to him by the
warmth of its expression of gratitude.
It then became my duty to appoint to the office of Grand Lecturer.
In doing so I was fully aware of the importance of the appointment. I
gave full consideration to the requirements of the office and appointed
to succeed Brother Davis an outstanding member of the Ritual Committee, Worshipful Brother Donald G. Campbell, who has rendered great
service as Assistant Grand Lecturer, of the 5th Division. The now, Very
Worshipful Donald G. Campbell whose appointment became effective
on January 1, 1960. has shown, in his nine months of service as such
Grand Lecturer that his appointment was fully justified. I am completely
satisfied with his service as such.
His appointment resulted in a vacancy in the office of Assistant
Grand Lecturer in the 5th Division, and I therefore appointed Worshipful Brother Ralph W. Collins, who had been serving as Inspector of
the 5 l 5th Masonic District for some years, and in whom I have great
confidence.

REVOCATION OF EDICT OF MARCH 25TH, 1957
On March 25th, 1957, the Grand Master, M.W.L. Harold Anderson, issued an Edict enjoining masons in California from becoming. or
remaining, members of a certain Shrine Club of San Jose, "until this
order shall be modified, revoked or rescinded by the Grand Master or
by the Grand Lodge of California ... "
This Edict was approved by the Grand Lodge at its 1957 Annual
Communication.
Upon representations to me that the conduct of the brethren involved had been corrected and the abuses terminated, at the request of

After the receipt of the written statements required by me. and with
the approval of Past Grand Master Anderson. and of the Deputy Grand
Master and the Grand Wardens, by edict on February 10th, 1960. I
undertook to rescind the injunction pronounced by Past Grand Master
Anderson.
My authority to so rescind the Edict aforesaid has been questioned
by the Chairman of the Committee on Jurisprudence, and I believe that
this Grand Lodge should determine the matter. If. in his Edict of March
25th, 1957, the then Grand Master had not used the language: "until
this order shall be modified, revoked or rescinded by the Grand Master,
or by the Grand Lodge of California" I certainly would not have presumed to terminate it. But the Grand Lodge, with the approval of the
Committee on Jurisprudence, adopted it with that very language in the
Resolution presented by the Committee on Jurisprudence, and in my
opinion, by retaining that language, the Grand Lodge authorized the
Grand Master to modify, revoke or rescind the Edict. I feel therefore
that the Grand Lodge would be wise to adopt one of two courses of
action: I. Approve my Edict of February I 0th, 1960, or 2. Revoke and
rescind the Edict of March 25th. 1957.

DECISIONS
During the course of the year many problems have been presented
to me which required interpretations of our Masonic law. I list herein
those of my decisions which may be of interest or assistance to my
brethren.
(Decisions 5, 6, I 0, 11, 13. and 20 were withdrawn by the Grand
Master.)
1. May a Lodge pay fees to brethren of the Lodge or to brethren of
another Lodge as compensation for their services as Acting Master
or Acting Chaplain in conducting a masonic funeral service for a
deceased mason?
My answer was no. I noted an exception that if the Acting Chaplain be an ordained minister, and if he be requested to officiate as
such minister, it would be proper to pay him a reasonable sum for
his services.

24

25

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

2. May the Master of a Lodge appoint to the office of Chaplain of
the Lodge, a Mason who is not a member of the Lodge?
My answer was no. The Chaplain must be a member of the Lodge
which he serves as Chaplain.

14. Mus t the auditing committee appointed by the M aster, a t each
stated meeting, audit the bills presented for payment, or may the
bills be paid with the consent of the Lodge, without audit by such
committee?

3. May a Lodge, in lieu of providing flowers for an ill brother , or for
the funeral services for a deceased brother. make a contribution of
an amount equal to the cost of such flowers to a Shrine Hospital?
My answer was no.

I ruled that the bills must be examined and reported on by the
auditing committee before they could be authorized paid. The
Lodge has authority to order that the bills be paid or not paid,
contrary to the recommendation of the said committee, but must
have the report of the committee before acting upon the bills.

4. Is a Board of Trustees, elected by a Lodge under the authority of
Section 405, California Masonic Code, authorized tG dispose of
Lodge funds without reference to or control by the Lodge?
My answer was no. Such a Board of Trustees must. in its administration of Lodge funds or property remain completely under the
control of the Lodge.
7. I was asked if it would be in contravention of Masonic law for
members of the Jobs Daughters to sell tickets to a public event,
when each purchaser of a ticket at the price of $1.00 would become
entitled to a chance to win merchandise of val ue from $50.00 to
$300.00, as a result of a drawing by chance.
I ruled that such a project was a lottery and would be in violation
not only of our masonic law but also of the California Penal Code
and could not therefore be countenanced by the Grand Lodge.

8. Is an applicant for the degree of masonry disqualified because of
a prior conviction of a felony, even though after serving a prison
term for such felony he had received an unconditional pardon from
the Governor of Cali fornia?
My answer was that he is disqualified.
9. I was asked i.f a man who had been raised to the sublime degree
of M aster Mason in a California lodge by courtesy request from
the Grand Lodge of Germany, which Grand Lodge was a t that
time in fraterna l relationship with our Grand Lodge, could be
received by that California lodge by a ffiliation, his petition for
affiliation having been presented to the lodge subsequent to the
termination of our recognition of the Grand Lodge of Germany.
My answer was that the Lodge could not elect him and that until
fraternal relations with the United Grand Lodge of Germany be
restored, his only course to obtain membership in a California
Lodge would be to sever his relation with the lodge in Germany and
petition the California Lodge for the degrees.
12. May printed or written invitations be sent to the brethren to attend the conferring of a degree upon a named candidate?
My answer was no. The candidate's name must not appear on any
such notice.

15. Is it contrary to masonic law or regulations to manufacture and
sell ash trays bearing the square and compass or other masonic
emblems?
I held that such conduct would be in contravention of our law and
that even though such merchandise be given away it would be in
the utmost bad taste.
16. May a Lodge collect funds from its members and hold such funds
in trust for scholarship grants?
My answer was no. Lodges may establish trust funds only for
purposes which have direct connection with the business and welfare of the particular Lodge, and a trust fund fo r scholarship
grants does not operate for such purpose. Such a course would,
no doubt, result in many conflicting variations in handling such
trust funds among the many Lodges throughout the Jurisdiction
and result in grave con fusion and embarrassment. A brother desiring to make contributions for scholarship awards may satisfy
that desire by making them to the Tru stees of the Masonic H omes
who are already in a position to sequester and administer such
contributions for such a purpose.
17. I was asked if our Grand Lodge could properly enter into a project
to establish a home for the a ged, in which aged masons, their
wives and widows might be cared for upon payment by them of
amounts of money sufficient, or more than sufficient to care fo r
them during their lives.
My answer was that while such projects have been sponsored by
several other organizations, possibly with considerable success
and profit to the sponsors. such projects are probably not charitable ones, at least not in the sense of our understanding of the
meaning of the words "masonic charity." The Grand Lodge of
California operates the Masonic Homes of California as Masonic
Charities , and the Grand Lodge should not become financially
involved in such a project as that suggested by the brethren who
propounded the question.

RESOLUTIONS

PROCLAMATION
CONSTITUTION OBSERVANCE

To all Masonic Brethren within the Jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge
of California:
To commemorate the one hundred seventy-third anniversary of the
signing of the Constitution of the United States of America, that
momentous event on September 17th, 1787, I do hereby designate the
month of September, 1960 as Constitution Observance Month.
I direct that each Lodge in this Grand Jurisdiction shall, during the
month of September or October, 1960, preferably during September.
either independently or in conjunction with other Lodges set apart at
least one day to memQrialize this occasion.
I direct that when more than one Lodge shall join in the same program for the purpose stated. none of said Lodges shall hold a meeting
or schedule any event for the Lodge on the day appointed for this
observance.
I suggest that it is desirable that the program or programs planned
shall be community events, open to the public, and held in such suitable
building. park or place available and appropriate for such observance,
and which may be readily accessible to the public.
Emphasis should be given to the history, origin and interpretation
of the provisions, as well as the language of the Constitution, and the
intent of lits framers.
This great document which outlines the system for the preservation
of human liberty and human rights. the written guarantee of American
free institutions and American liberties is the greatest political document of all time.
Edmund Burke. the great English champion of liberty is credited
with the statement:
"ALL THAT IS NECESSARY FOR THE TRIUMPH OF
EVIL IS FOR ENOUGH GOOD MEN TO DO NOTHING."
My brethren, let us each be vigilent.
Dated: June l, 1960.
Attest:
LLOYD E. WILSON
Grand Secretary

The Grand Secretary presented the following resolutions which were

MASTER MASONS' ATTENDANCE
(A-2)

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. 6 A. M. of California:
WHEREAS. under the present provisions of Section 103 of California Masonic Code, Master Masons are prohibited from attending the
opening of Grand Lodge at the Annual Communication; and
WHEREAS, our Temple facilities at the present time now make it
possible to have a larger group in attendance: and
WHEREAS. Grand Lodge consists of representatives of all the
Master Masons in this jurisdiction,
NOW THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED: That Section 103 of
California Masonic Code be amended to read as follows:
"Section 103. Who may be present at opening and election. None but
members of the Grand Lodge, the Grand Officers, Past Grand Officers
and Representatives of other Grand Lodges, shall be present during an
election at the Annual Communication. Master Masons may be present
at all other times during the Annual Communication and at all Special
Communications."
Respectfully submitted,
ALFRED F. BRESLAUER, Past Master, Lodge No. 344
Referred to Committees on Jurisprudence, and on Policy and General
Purposes.

of representation in Grand Lodge, be repealed.

REQUIREMENTS FOR CHARTER
(A-9)

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, the formation of new lodges in California is for the
purpose of advancing Freemasonry: and
WHEREAS, it is not advisable to start a new lodge in areas in
which the number of potential members is too small to support a regular
lodge: and
WHEREAS, a lodge under dispensation should establish its ability
to perform the quties of a regular lodge before applying for a charter:
and
WHEREAS, a lodge should be situated in an area where it can
expect to continue to show a desirable growth in membership:
NOW THEREFORE IT IS RESOLVED: That the California
Masonic Code be amended by striking from Section 62 the words:
··No charter shall be granted to any lodge until it shall have worked
a time under dispensation."
and substituting therefor the words:
"No charter shall be granted to any lodge until it shall have worked
under dispensation for a minimum of six ( 6) months and have initiated,
passed and raised at least two ( 2 ) candidates."
Respectfully submitted,
HARRY E. HART, Master, Lodge No. 749
HARRISON F. TAYLOR, Master, Lodge No. 658
ELMER G. NORDMAN, Master, Lodge No. 99
Referred to Committees on Jurisprudence, and on Policy and General
Purposes.

NATIONAL ANTHEM

INSTALLATION REQUIREMENT S

(B-1)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. 8 A. M. of California:
WHEREAS. by an act of Congress on March 3, 1931, The StarSpangled Banner was designated as our National Anthem, and
WHEREAS. we should be proud of our National Anthem, and
WHEREAS. this should be the only proper musical piece that
should be played or sung when our National Emblem is displayed,
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED: That our ritual be
amended, Monitor page 56, Sec. 554 of CMC, that "The Brethren will
join in singing one verse of America," be deleted and there be inserted
in its place the following, "The Brethren will join in singing one verse
of our Nation Anthem, The Star-Spangled Banner."

INSPECTORS' DUTIES
(B-2)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. 8 A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, subdivision 10th of section 161 of the California
Masonic Code makes it the duty of the Inspector to examine the books
and records of each Lodge to determine if its manner of transacting business, making its returns; and paying its Grand Lodge dues conform to
our laws, and to report to the Grand Master the result thereof at the
same time as he makes his annual report to the Grand Lecturer: and
WHEREAS, the sufficiency of the Lodge's returns and payment of
Grand Lodge dues have been supervised by the Grand Secretary for
many years,
BE IT RESOLVED, that subdivision 10th of section 161 of the
California Masonic Code be amended to read as follows:
"To examine the books and reports of each Lodge to determine if
its manner of transacting its business conforms to our laws, and to report
to the Grand Master any violations of law."
Respectfully submitted,
ELBERT W. DAVIS, Past Master, Lodge No. 571
Referred to Committees on Jurisprudence, and on Ritual.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. 8 A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, Section 324-A Ordinances, reads as follows:
"Where the installation of Officers is to take place in a building other
than where the Lodge regularly meets, the Lodge should open in the
Lodge room and repair to the place of installation."
WHEREAS, some Lodges meet in a small Lodge room, being inadequate to accommodate the members and friends who wish to attend
the installation ceremony.
WHEREAS, a Lodge opens in its regular rooms then repairs to the
place of installation, after the ceremony is over journeys back to the
regular Lodge room to close Lodge, this means many miles of unnecessary travel, as usually the Officers and members again journey back to
the place of installation to enjoy the rest of the evening with their family
and friends and to see that they get home safely.
WHEREAS, many installations are held on a night other than the
regular Lodge night and their regular room is not available on that night.
BE IT THEREFORE RESOLVED. that Section 324-A, Ordinances, be amended, by adding after the word installation, "a Lodge
may open and close in the room designated as the place of installation."
Respectfully submitted,
JoHN D. BOWMAN, Past Master, Lodge No. 764
C. THOMAS LouDON, Past Master, Lodge No. 764
PAUL A. BASTING, Master, Lodge No. 764
JOHN H. Cox.Past Master, Lodge No. 764
Referred to Committees on Jurisprudence, and on Policy and General

FUNERAL SERVICE LIMITATION
(B-4)

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. 8 A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, Lodges and Masters of this jurisdiction are being requested to conduct Masonic funerals for suspended members, and
WHEREAS, Section 740 of the California Masonic Code defines
suspension of a Mason as being "A deprivation of all his rights and
privileges as such, and prohibits all Masons and Lodges from holding
any Masonic intercourse with him until he shall be legally restored," and
WHEREAS, Section 581 (d) CMC states, "A Mason dying
under sentence of suspension, cannot be restored by any action subsequent to his death," and

44

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

WHEREAS, Section 604 CMC states, "Every Mason who dies in
good standing is entitled to burial with Masonic honors," and

PROFICIENCY REQUIREMENT

WHEREAS, the latter part of the same section ( 604, CMC) and
Section 605 ( i.) CMC states, "One suspended for non-payment of dues,
nothing else appearing against him may be buried with Masonic honors.
The Master may call the Lodge together, at the request of any number
of brethren to determine if such action should be taken, or without such
request if he believes such action should be taken, etc."
WHEREAS, these statements would appear to be contradictory and
would tend to validate a double standard, and
WHEREAS, the Masters and brethren are put in an arbitrary position of deciding on the suitability of a suspended member's past conduct
on short notice, particularly where the member in question is not a
member of the Lodge in the place where he resides or a member of this
jurisdiction, and
WHEREAS, the reasons for a Master Mason's suspension are due
to his neglect and refusal to live up to his obligations, and
WHEREAS, there is little reason for his suspension for N.P.D. in
that he is required only to contact the Master or Secretary of his
Lodge and inform them of his reasons for his inability, and
WHEREAS, his dues can be remitted or paid by the members of his
Lodge in order that a worthy Brother Mason will not be lost to the
Craft, and
WHEREAS, the families of suspended members request Masonic
funerals for members who have been under suspension for periods up to
ten years for N.P.D., and said requests place the Master of a Lodge
in an arbitrary position should he refuse, therefore
BE IT RESOLVED, that the portion of Section 605. i, and Section
604 relating to the burial of members suspended be stricken from the
CMC in order that deserving Brethren may receive proper respect at the
final call.
F. E. FINLEY, Master, Lodge No. 45
GusTAVE W. KLOTZ, Past Master. Lodge No. 45
LoRNE E. WEAVER, Past Master, Lodge No. 45

(B-6)

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, question fifteen on the Application for Degrees requiring the applicant to promise that he will not apply for or receive any
degree or be initiated in any Lodge, Order or Organization, the prerequisite of membership wherein is that a person be a Master Mason,
until he has given satisfactory evidence, by strict examination in open
Lodge, that he is entirely proficient and well-qualified in the Candidate's
Lecture of the Degree of Master Mason and in no event within twelve
months after he has received the Degree of Master Mason, has not
accomplished the true purpose, and
WHEREAS, we feel. that the Third Degree proficiency should be
mandatory before a member is entitled to a dues card or the rights and
privileges of a Master Mason,
THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that question fifteen be omitted from the Application for Degrees.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that a member is not entitled to
a dues card or the rights and privileges of a Master Mason (except
funeral services) until he is entirely proficient and well-qualified in the
Candidate's Lecture of the Degree of Master Mason, and that this must
be accomplished within six months, or automatic suspension will prevail,
unless further time shall be granted by a vote of the Lodge.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that the Master's Congratulation
be required at 'the completion of the Third Degree proficiency, rather
than following the Third Degree Charge.
Respectfully submitted,
JoHN R. GREGORY, Master, Lodge No. 736
ROBERT HousH, Senior Warden. Lodge No. 736
CHESTER T. HOBBS, Junior Warden. Lodge No. 736
Referred to Committee on Policy and General Purposes.

To the Most Worship ful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
WHERE AS, the Junior Warden of each constituent Lodge of this
jurisdiction, by tradition , general usage, and ritualistic direction at the
time of his installation, has been entrusted with the superintendence of
the Craft during the hours of refreshment, and
WHERE AS, such superintendence customarily included the proper
expendit ure of refreshm ent funds for the purpose not only of actual
refreshments but also for fraternal intercourse with other Lodges and
other social purposes, and
WHERE AS, the Junior Warden , by virtue of his required knowl~
edge of Masonic law and by his years of previous experience as a line
officer is suitably equipped to administer Lodge funds for the above
purpose, and
WHERE AS, this Grand Lodge in 1958 established a "revolvin g
fund of not more than $100.00 for the use of the Steward s in providing
refreshments for all regular Lodge functions," and
WHERE AS, many Lodges have continue d to entrust this responsi~
bility to their Junior Warden s as proper and responsible senior officers,
and
WHERE AS, such financial responsibity without revolving funds
has in many cases caused financial hardship s to those Junior Warden s
without ample resources,
THERE FORE, BE IT RESOL VED: That Section 401 of the Cali~
fomia Masonic Code be amended by inserting in line eleven after the
word "Stewar ds" the following, "or Junior Warden as the Master may
determine.''
Respectfully submitted,
LowELL H. BECKENDORF, Past Master, Lodge No. 462
MELVIN S. SPRINGER, Past Master, Lodge No. 462

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:

young men; and

and in cooperation with Brother Wakefield Taylor of that Committee,
the Grand Secretary presents the following for consideration by the

Section 574 of the 'Masonic Code be amended in paragraph 3 by
substituting the words "in accordance with the provisions of Section
404 of this Code" in place of the words "in securities legal for savings
banks, under either the laws of the State of California or the laws of
the State of Hawaii."
Respectfully submitted
LLOYD E. WILSON, Past Master, Lodge No. 630
Referred to Committee on Jurisprudence.

48

WHEREAS, the Principles upon which it is founded are of the
highest, religious, moral. ethical. and patriotic nature in that it teaches
Belief in a Supreme Being, Love and Honor to Parents, Honest Toil,
Loyalty to Ideals and Friends, Courteousness, Gentlemanliness, Patriotism in Peace as well as War, Cleanliness in Mind and Body, Good
Citizenship, and
WHEREAS. a number of Constituent Lodges within the Jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of California have indicated an enthusiastic
interest in sponsoring a chapter or chapters of the Order of DeMolay,
and
WHEREAS, Freemasonry and Freemasons are and always have
been devoted to the Building and Development of Character, Leadership and Good Citizenship among men and Nations;
NOW THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED: that any Constituent
Lodge or group of Lodges within the Jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge
of California be hereby authorized to sponsor a chapter or chapters
of the Order of DeMolay: and
That such Lodge or Group of Lodges Sponsoring a Chapter or
Chapters of DeMolay be hereby authorized to expend, with the approval
of the Lodge, such sums as are reasonably necessary to assist a Chapter
or Chapters, such expenditures to be taken from current Lodge funds
only, and not to exceed one third ( Y3) of the amount of the refreshment
fund currently allowed by Grand Lodge.
Respectfully submitted,

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. 6 A. M. of California:
With the approval of the Grand Lodge Committee on Jurisprudence,
and in cooperation with Brother Wakefield Taylor of that Committee,
the Grand Secretary presents the following for consideration by the
1960 Annual Communication:
Section 432 of the Masonic Code be amended so that provisions
6 and 7 will read as follows:
"Suspension for non-payment of dues or otherwise or expulsion of a multiple member shall immediately, and of itself, terminate his membership in all Lodges in this jurisdiction, and the
Secretary of any Lodge in this jurisdiction suspending or expelling such a member shall immediately notify the Grand Secretary
and also every other Lodge in which the multiple member holds
membership. Like notice shall be given in case of reinstatement,
which shall immediately and automatically restore him to membership in every other Lodge in this jurisdiction of which he was
a member."
"Nothing in this section shall be construed to prevent a multiple member from receiving a certificate of discontinuance of
multiple membership as provided in Section 453 if otherwise entitled to the same."
Section 432 be amended by substituting the word "multiple" in place

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

of the word "plural" in provisions 4, 5, and 9: and by adding to provision 8 the following: A multiple membership as used in this section
means and is defined to be either dual or plural membership.

Section 453 be amended by substituting the word "multiple" in
place of the word "plural."
Respectfully submitted,

REPORT OF GRAND TREASURER
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
In presenting my sixth annual report as your Grand Treasurer covering the fiscal year ended June 30, 1960, I do so with continued gratitude
and appreciation to this Grand Lodge for allowing me the privilege of
serving in this capacity.
In compliance with Section 146 of the California Masonic Code, the
Grand Treasurer is required, in addition to other duties:
To make at each Annual Communication, a detailed report of his
receipts and disbursements, supported by proper vouchers for the
latter, and to present a statement of the existing condition of its
property and finances.
Supporting vouchers are available in the Grand Secretary's office.
This year again, through the cooperation of all concerned, we have
combined all published flnancial reports into one report. The financial
reports included herein cover:
1. Summary of Receipts and Disbursements - Comparative year
ended June 30, 1960, and year ended June 30, 1959.
2. Grand Lodge F. & A. M. and Exhibits.
3. Grand Lodge F. & A. M. Statement of 1960 Annual Returns.
4. Masonic Homes of California, including the Permanent Endowment Fund.
5. California Masonic Memorial Temple.
Respectfully submitted,
EDWARD H. SIEMS,
Grand Treasurer
Referred to Committee on Distribution.

REPOR T OF THE GRAN D SECRE TARY
To the Most Worship ful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
I have the honor to present to you herewith my Nineteen th Annual
Report as your Grand Secretar y.
UNFINISHED BUSINESS
The following matters were continued from the last Annual Communication to the present one:
1. Cemeter y Recommendations, pages 205 and 209, 1959 Proceedings.
2. Grand Lecturer 's Recommendations, page 75, 1959 Proceedings.
3. Research Recommendations, page 200, 1959 Proceedings.
4. Resolution on Indemni ty, page 32, 1959 Proceedings.
5. York Rite Sovereig n College, page 19, 1959 Proceedings.
CHANGE OF MEETING PLACE
York Lodge No. 423 has changed its meeting place from South Gate
to Walnut Park. Sunrise Lodge No. 522 has changed its meeting place
from Los Angeles to Montere y Park. Jordan Lodge No. 654 has
changed its meeting place from Los Angeles to Walnut Park.
It is recommended that the Charters of the nine Hawaiia n Lodges
which were located in the Territor y of Hawaii at the time the Lodge
was constitut ed be endorsed to show the location as the State of Hawaii.
These change of meeting places have been officially approved under
the authority of the Grand Master, and the Grand Secretar y now requests authority to properly endorse their Charters .
LoDGES UNDER DISPENSATION
The following Lodges under dispensation were instituted subseque nt
to August 1, 1959, and prior to June 30:
Ashland , Bay Claire Vista, Rio Hondo, Koolau and Yucca Valley.
Each of these Lodges collected only an equal or a less amount of dues
than the per capita tax, and in accord with preceden t the Grand Master,
at our suggestion, directed that they be not required to pay the per
capita tax. It is respectfully requeste d that this be approved .

MEMBERSHIP
Those who carefully read the Proceedi ngs know that for the past
several years I have analyzed our membership experience with ~he
thought in mind that we will not only know what has been happenm g
but what we may reasonab ly anticipate.
This year I J'resent comparison figures for the last forty years by
ten year periods commencing with 1920.
In 1920 and again in 1950, which are immediate post war years, we
initiated the largest numbers, but even so in 1960 we initiated more than
in 1930 and 1940. The same general proportio n holds true for the
number raised. One of the encouraging signs is that we have the largest
number of affiliates of any time in this block of years, and it may well be
due to the excellent -work of the Sojourne rs Committee of Grand Lodge.
The number suspende d for non-paym ent of dues gives cause for
concern, because while it is less than 1930 and 1940 it is within 100 of
being twice as many as in 1950. The loss by death is at its highest peak
and that, of course, can be expected with the greater number of members
and advancin g years.
The net gain is the lowest of the years with the exception of 1940
when it was an actual loss of 554. Many Grand Lodges have been suffering losses for years. Taking into account all the factors which I reported
last year, on page 52 of the 1959 Proceedings, I think we may take comfort in the fact that we still show a gain.

REPORT OF THE GRAND LECTURE R
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F . & A . M. of California:
The report of the Grand Lecturer is not an individual report of his
activities or of the Ritual Committee itself. It is, rather, a report to the
Grand Lodge of its own progress in maintaining the purity of our work
in the conferring of the degrees of Masonry.
The Masters and Wardens of the Lodges are. in the last analysis,
the true custodians of the ritual. The manner in which the light of
Masonry is brought to our initiates rests ultimately with them. A knowledge and appreciation of the beauties of Masonry is a prime requisite
for the officers of a Lodge. Through them, and through the Coaches,
the Master spreads the light of Masonic education. If they are not
schooled, if they are not proficient, if they do not possess a knowledge
of the art, they cannot do a proper job of inculcating those wise and
serious truths which have been our bulwark through generations.
To guide, counsel and direct this teaching is the assigned task of the
Ritual Committee. The Grand Lecturer and the Assistant Grand
Lecturers met in San Francisco on December 4th to 6th. 1959, under
the direction of Very Worshipful Elbert W. Davis, now Past Grand
Lecturer. All the work of the three degrees, including the Masters and
Candidates Lectures, was exemplified. Most Worshipful Arthur M.
Warren. Past Grand Master and Past Grand Lecturer, was present,
as he has been in the past, and consented to act as candidate. We all
hope that he w,ill be joined in the future by the Junior Past Grand
Lecturer.
In view of Bill's then announced retirement and the impending appointment of a new Grand Lecturer, Worshipful Ralph W. Collins,
Inspector of the 515th District, was in attendance. He and Worshipful
Harold N. Richards, newly appointed to the Second Division as Assistant Grand Lecturer. proved their qualifications for the appointments.
On January I. 1960, it became my privilege to serve by appointmen t
balance of Bill's term as Grand Lecturer.
the
for
In order to further develop a close and harmonious understandi ng
among the members of the Committee and to discuss problems which
might be of general interest, a meeting was held in Bakersfield, arranged
by Assistant Grand Lecturer Raymond G. Taylor. on February 20th
and 21st. The scope of problems brought for discussion illustrated
clearly the manifold duties of the Assistant Grand Lecturers. In addition to the ritualistic schools, the Assistant Grand Lecturers have, for
several years, been charged with the responsibility of supervising the
arrangemen ts and appointing qualified members of Grand Lodge to fill
vacancies for the various ceremonies requiring the opening of Grand
Lodge. Perhaps of greater importance is the availability of the Assistant

Grand Lecturer, in his division, to work with the Inspectors and Lodge
Officers to maintain that good order so essential to the peace and

feeling that in the divisional and district organization we have untapped
resources for bringing the Grand Lodge program to fruition. We are
fortunate in having the services of these dedicated men as the Masonic
leaders in each Division. I am certain that the Inspectors feel too that
in this group are men who can be relied upon as problems are confronted.
I have been impressed by the reports of schools held, of lod.se visitations. and of District Officers Association meetings held by our Inspectors. An average of two schools for each degree has become the
expected number and those who conduct fewer are a small minority.
Officers Associations exist in all but a few scattered districts. In addition to these matters, full support is being given the Endowment
Fund, the Memorial Temple Campaign and all other programs of Grand
Lodge. The results are apparent and the truth that leadership begets
leadership is apparent in the results, both ritualistic and in the health
of the Lodges. To be an Inspector in the Grand Lodge of California
is a consuming task and I pay homage to those men who are truly the
backbone of Masonry.
The challenge of Masonry today lies not in the revolution of our
system but rather in its perfection so that the man who knocks on our
door receives an opportunity to grow in moral understanding. The
continuing zeal of the Masters and the officers whom they direct, the
Coaches, the Inspectors and the Ritual Committee will not only maintain the present high standard but will carry our institution to new
heights.
To have had the opportunity of serving as Assistant Grand Lecturer
under Bill Davis was a rare privilege. As friendship and understanding
grew, I found him to be a warm and real person, without pretense or
subterfuge. Courage in great measure, an ability to inspire his subordinates, and, above all, a knowledge of and love for our ritual and the
craft made his tenure as Grand Lecturer a memorable one. To continue to have his wise counsel will give his successor and the Ritual
Committee added strength. As Junior Past Grand Lecturer, he joins
a distinguished group and adds his measure of lustre to it.
The courtesies and help extended the Ritual Committee by the
Grand Secretary, the Assistant Grand Secretary and the entire office
are too many to enumerate. Without this understanding assistance we
could not function properly.
To our Grand Master and friend, Most Worshipful Joe L. Shell,
goes the hope that our assignments have been carried out in a creditable
manner and the thanks of the Ritual Committee for his trust and
support.
Respectfully submitted,
DoN G. CAMPBELL

Islands are still feeling the effects of lessened population but are maintaining, in their leadership, a splendid zeal for Masonry. I am sure

soon on the other Islands and will find the Lodges ready for their appointed task.

This Communication will conclude the term of Brother Ralph H.
Head as a member of our Board of Trustees.
Legislation adopted in 1948 increased the Board to nine members
and placed a limitation on the number of consecutive terms of service.
Past Grand Master Edward H. Siems, the then Grand Master
selected Brother Head to serve on the newly expanded Board. Since
that time he has given yeoman service and is responsible for many of the
constructive policies which have made our Homes operation a model to
which other Grand Lodges aspire. Since 1958, he has served as Vice
President.
In addition to his manifold duties as Trustee he has acted as our
representative on the Investment Committee which has done such an
outstanding service in handling the funds of Grand Lodge. His administrative ability and knowledge of finance and real estate have been of
tremendous value to those in charge of this important function.
As a further recognition of his ability Brother Ralph served as
Grand Orator during the term of Past Grand Master L. Harold Anderson in 1957.
We thank Brother Ralph for his unselfish service, confident that
future Grand Masters will find a place for the talents of this faithful
servant.
MASONIC HOME AT UNION CITY ( DECOTO)

The Masonic Homes of California received bids for a Hospital
Facility at the Masonic Home in Union City (formerly Decato) from
a selected list of six contractors on March 25, 1959. Swinerton and
Walberg contractors of San Francisco and Oakland with a low bid of
$1,183,3~5.00 were awarded the Contract on April 9th. The Contract
for the Hospital included a new adjoining transformer vault and switch
board room, changes in electric services, changes in main water service,
a new stainless steel range hood, stack and fan in existing kitchen, and
a new fire alarm system in all the buildings of the Home. The area of
the building not including terraces was approximately 50,000 square
feet, or approximately $22.00 per square foot. The total number of
beds was 131 of which number, 7 were in single bedrooms and 124 were
in two bed wards. The cost per bed was approximately $8,400.00. Construction work began April 20, 1959 and the final date of completion
and acceptance was June 8, 1960, the Contractor having been allowed
six weeks extension of time lost due to strikes, rain, etc.
The Masonic Home is located on a 267 acre site but the buildings
were placed on an area of high ground which is limited in size. In the
interest of economy and convenience, it was necessary to locate the
hospital with respect to access from the main kitchen, from the Home
itself, from the Nurses Home, and for deliveries. ambulance and auto-

86

87

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRANO LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

mobile. Availability of main service lines for gas, water and electricity
was considered. To meet all requirements, it was necessary to carve
the site out of a broken rock hillside with extreme variations in elevations of grades of over 50 feet. Advantage was taken of the grades,
however, to produce outdoor protected terraces at the first, second
and third floor levels. Service entrances were provided at the ground
floor level, a nurses entrance and entrance from the existing home via
a covered bridge at the second floor level and a terrace entrance at the
third floor level.
Patients arrive by car or ambulance at the first floor street entrance
or by wheel stretchers or wheel chairs from the Home across the
covered bridge, and are taken to the assigned floor by a hospital
elevator.
Food is prepared in the main kitchen for the Home, across the street,
transported in heated food carts to the hospital second floor diet kitchen
where it is served and transported in heated tray carts to the rooms.
Each floor has a small diet kitchen for the preparation of snacks between
meals.
The average age of patients in this hospital is well over 80 years.
Their ills are mostly such as associated with people of that age. Medical
care for the institution is provided by contract with the Palo Alto Clinic
at Palo Alto, California. Any cases requiring major surgery are transported to the Palo Alto-Stanford University Hospital Center. Doctors
visit the institution at regular intervals during the week and upon call.
In this new unit, space is provided for a medical unit on the first floor
consisting of a doctors consultation room, two examination rooms with
four dressing cubicles, a minor surgery or treatment room of major
surgery size and complete with doctors' scrub-up. sterilizers, portable
x-ray, developing cabinet, view box, cast room, table, instrument
storage cabinet, and spot light. Adjacent to the treatment room is a
dental room and a Laboratory.
The buildinq is five stories, Type 1 construction, fireproof, and earthquake proof. The ground floor has an equipment room, clean and
soiled linen rooms, garbage, and general storage space. The first floor
has a nurses lounge, men and women visitor's toilets, nurses station,
medical rooms, patient rooms. baths with lifts, tubs and showers and
necessary utility rooms and linen closets. The second, third and fourth
floors are bed room floors with all the necessary service rooms, such as
baths, utility, storage, and day rooms.
Each day room has a TV, an aquarium, pictures and colorful chairs.
Each patient bed has a head or pillow phone connection for choice of
two radio stations. Each room has glass and screen sliding doors opening upon either a terrace or a 4'-6" wide balcony. The first floor has
16 beds, the second 31, the third and fourth floors 42 beds each. Each
bed room and ward is equipped with new, modern hospital furniture

consisting of Simmons hospital beds with Serta mattresses, over-bed
cable with dressing and shaving compartments, night stands and colorful
chairs. Each patient has a small wardrobe for clothes and personal
effects. Each bed can be enclosed with pastel-colored cubicle curtains
for privacy if so desired. Rooms are painted in pastel colors and have
spun glass draw drapes.
All rooms are air conditioned to maintain as nearly as possible a
constant temperature during summer and winter. In case of a power
failure, a Diesel engine power plant will produce emergency lighting
for corridors and elsewhere as required. The water for the entire home
is supplied by wells on the property and pumped to a tank on an
adjacent hill. Due to hardness of this water, softners were installed
under this Contract.
Furniture and equipment for the hospital was purchased in March
1960 but due to factory conditions, delivery on some items was delayed.
This, together with a break-in period for equipment, delayed the occupancy of the building until August 23, on which date 80 patients
were moved from the old hospital.
fo recent years the Codes and Regulations governing hospitals and
homes for the aged have been materially changed. Each year before
9ranting a permit to operate the Home an examination and inspection
of the Home buildings was made by the State Authorities. After several
criticisms of some conditions, the demand was made by the licensing
authorities that certain changes be made this year in the Home. Drawings and Specifications for the necessary changes were made, submitted
to the State for approval and a contract signed with the lowest bidder,
M. H. Sjoberg and Son, of Oakland, at a cost of $83,771.00. The
changes required were the enclosing of the main central stair way in the
Administration Building with fireproof walls and doors to form a smoke
free tower in case of fire, the installation of emergency lighting in
corridors and the installation of an intercommunicating system for each
room in the home, with the exception of the old hospital unit which
would be subject to changes when vacated. It is now possible with
this system installed for each room to call the attendant in the Main
Lobby in case of illness or emergency. In order to complete the additions and alterations, it was necessary to make changes in conduits
and electrical wiring as well as changes in doors and closets in some
rooms. Electrical panels were installed in the Administration Building
lobby to record calls from rooms. It also became necessary at this time
to add additional telephone lines in the plant. This contract was completed and accepted on the same day as the Hospital acceptance.
A circular terrace on the front of the Administration Building had
settled during a period of years, opening up a horizontal crack approximately i inches wide in the masonry. The Main Building wall showed
no distress and the assumption was that the foundations of the main

88

building were carried to fl.rm bearing but the terrace foundations were
on fill. It therefore became necessary to underpin the terrace with
caissons carried down approximately 20 feet and rebuild the masonry
wall above grade. The metal railing around this terrace had rusted
at the level of the concrete floor slab and this was repaired, replaced,
and painted.
After the completion of the above additions and alterations the
State approval was granted on all the work without criticism.
COVINA

Over forty years ago far-sighted Masonic Homes Trustees selected
the present location of the Home for Children at Covina, green acres
on the far outskirts of a sleepy little town miles from downtown Los
Angeles. With the natural growth of such things the Masonic Home
location became a suburb of Covina, and is now an urban part of the
great growing community called Greater Los Angeles.
The forty acres of the Home are now almost completely surrounded
by bright new homes from which emit each morning a stream of
children which fill the local public schools to over-flowing. Because of
the affinity between California Freemasonry and the public schools,
some of these children head for that portion of the Home which has
been set aside as temporary public school class rooms. The capable
superintendent, of the Home, Robert M. Henry is, quite coincidentally,
the President of the local Board of Education. This great spirit of cooperation has helped the district avoid half-day sessions and reduced
educational schedules.
Outside of having a built-in public school system at home, our
young citizens at Covina live perfectly normal lives, swim in a new
swimming pool courtesy of generous California Masons, spend vacation weeks camping in Yosemite, packing into the High Sierras, and
providing the local schools with student leadership, scholarship, and
athletes.
The farm program continues, our children do their daily chores,
partly as a duty and partly to earn spending money. This is the life
that certain men, practicing operative Masonry as well as speculative,
have provided for the future leaders of California.
FINANCE

A review of the annual audit will reveal a substantial reduction in
resources and investments. This is, of course, due to the construction
program reported last year and elsewhere in this report. Upwards of
$1,300,000 was expended to comply with regulations of the State
Welfare Department, Fire Marshal and other regulatory agencies. Our
properties are now in excellent condition and all of our bills are paid.
For the benefit of Grand Lodge we stress that all of this work was

89

done through the use of reserves which had been carefully accumulated
from bequests and contributions. No part of the per capita tax nor any
operating funds have been used. Likewise no portion of the Endowment Fund has been put into this program. We urge this information
be given to our membership.
We have reached deeply into our reserves and have transferred
from other earmarked funds to do this work. Appreciation is here expressed to those who have made direct contributions to the New
Hospital Fund. We urge those so disposed to continue to make contributions for this purpose in order that we may restore the transferred
funds to the original purposes for which they were intended.
Special credit should be given to the Grand Lodge Investment
Committee of which W. Paul A. Pflueger, Assistant Grand Treasurer,
is Chairman. They have given careful and dedicated service to their
assignment. A substantial portion of the funds provided for the New
Hospital came from profits resulting from the sale of securities. We
have enjoyed a healthy return on our investments plus a substantial increment in value. While it is true that the security markets have been
favorable, we have enjoyed good returns and profits without sacrificing
the conservative principles upon which this Committee operates. The
members of the Homes Board are unanimous in expressing their appreciation for this outstanding service.
Operating costs continue to rise and with the opening of our New
Hospital, we will be faced with additional expenses due to State requirements. We are meeting hourly wage rates and other working
conditions prevafent in both the East Bay and Southern California
employment markets. The operation of our Homes today is big business
and payrolls and services constitute our major expense. We are subject
to the pressures of industry and labor and the fact that we operate as
a charity does not relieve us of this heavy load. Strict attention to costs
is being initiated and we are making surveys into every operation to
keep down expenses without sacrificing the service and comforts which
we extend to our residents.
As anticipated, the fiscal year ending June 30, 1960, resulted in a
deficit of $196,830.36 before a $294,992.83 non-recurring gain from
eecurity sales. On the basis of last year's projection of a $200,000 operating deficit, we requested a per capita tax of $1.00 payable July 1 of
this year. This will provide approximately $120,000 of additional revenue for 1961. Even with this added income we will face an estimated
operating deficit of $150,000 for the coming fiscal period. The nonrecurring 1960 surplus of $98.162.47 will be carried forward to supplement operating revenue for the same period, thus reducing the anticipated deficit by that sum.
It must be borne in mind by reason of the sale of a good portion of
our securities, a marked decrease will take place in revenue from invest-

90

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

ments. This may result in a larger deficit than anticipated. However,
during the past two months some sizeable bequests have been received.
They have been added to our holdings and will replace some of the
investments sold to build the hospital.
There is no doubt in our minds that costs will not decline, and inasmuch as investment revenue is difficult to project, we request that a per
capita tax of $1.00 again be levied at this communication payable July
1, 1961.

REPORT OF SUPERINTENDENT - MASONIC HOME
AT UNION CITY (Decoto)
To the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California:
It is a pleasure and a privilege to submit my fifth annual report as
Superintendent of the Masonic Home at Union City (Decato) for the
year ending June 30, 1960.
This has been a most eventful year in the history of the Home, one
that will, I am sure, be remembered for years to come. The new Hospital
Facility was completed and the keys given to us on June 16, 1960. Immediately we started preparing for occupancy. The Trustees designated
July 30, 1960, as the date for dedication of the new Hospital Facility
with occupancy to be completed as promptly thereafter as possible.
The other work required by the State Welfare Board in the Home
itself has all been completed. This consisted of a communication system
to each room, a fire alarm system throughout all buildings, fire doors and
special fire retarding glass in central stairway. This work also required
remodeling the office and installation of a new and larger switchboard
which is necesary to have coverage 24 hours a day; also to answer emergency calls on the communicating system.
At the beginning of the fiscal year, there were 359 members in the
Home, consisting of 138 men and 221 women. During the year 37 men,
average age of 79.08 and 43 women, average age of 77.51 years were
admitted to the Home. There were 37 men, average age of 82.10 and 42
