There were 81 members confined to our Hospital on June 30, 1%0, of
which 70 are considered permanent. In addition there are 40 women on
the fourth floor north and east wings, who receive assistance with their
daily needs and under the Hospital supervision.
We are happy to report no changes in the Supervising Staff. Mrs.
Evangeline Adams, R.N., Hospital Supervisor; Mrs. Sara Paris, Matron:
Brother Roy Cain, Assistant to the Superintendent: Brother Fred Boyle,
Office Manager: Mr. Paul Reichert, Purchasing and Stock Control; Mr.
William Emmal, Chef; all have been cooperative and guided their various departments most efficiently and satisfactorily.
Rev. Martin L. Tonner has supervised our devotional services and
given spiritual guidance to all in the Hospital and the Home.
We are happy to report that Dr. Wayne Collins, Chiropodist began
giving the folks care of their fed on May 1, 1960. The members in the
Home are very happy with this service and well satisfied.
We have enjoyed entertainment in the auditorium, arranged by the
Lodges, Job's Daughters, DeMolay, Rainbow Girls and Eastern Star
Chapters, as well as other groups and organizations. To all of them we
extend our sincere appreciation. In addition 24 Lodges have conferred
degrees in the Temple for the benefit of our Brethren.
One of the high lights of the year was the visitation by and the reception for our Most Worshipful Grand Master Joe L. Shell on January 30,
1960. On this date also the Board of Trustees held their quarterly meeting and annual visit at the Home. It is always a pleasure to have them
with us.
On September 30, 1959, we had the pleasure of welcoming approximately 1400 members of Grand Lodge and wives. Also included were our
Most Worshipful Grand Master Phil N. Myers and several Grand
Lodge Officers to perform the ceremony of Laying the Corner Stone of
the Hospital Facility. During the year many of the Trustees on various
occasions visited the Home for an inspection and to view the construction
of the new building.

HOME MEMBER SHIP

As of June 30, 1960, the population of our Masonic Home Family
numbers forty-seven children -twenty- nine boys and eighteen girls.
During the fiscal year of 1959-60, six children have been admitted to the
Home. two boys and four girls. Fourteen children left the Home, three
graduati ng from high school and ten returning to their families. One
joined the Air Force. Two graduate s plan to continue their educatio n,
and the other graduate is planning to work temporarily, with the goal in
mind to save money to further her chosen professio n as a buyer of women's apparel.

VISITATIO NS

The visitations of Masonic Lodges and other organizati ons continues
under the visitation program established in previous years. Reservatio ns
for a maximum of four hundred visitors are made every Visitation Sun.day. which is the third Sunday of each month. Reservatio ns are filled not
further than a year in advance. The visitation program has been well received by the hundreds of Lodges making use of this medium to tell its
JDembership the true meaning of Masonic Benevolence. It is worthy of
aote that the policy of visitations on the Third Sunday of each month is
of immeasurable value in guarantee ing and providing the children the
benefits of relaxation and diversion from routine programs.
ALUMNI OF THE COVINA HOME

The Covina Alumni Reunion is observed on the Second Sunday in
September, and the Alumni Reunion Dinner in San Francisco is on the
Saturday preceding Grand Lodge. Sacramen to Alumni have participate d
with a picnic in June of this year. It is most enjoyable to meet on these
occasions which are especially set apart for the Alumni, and for fellowship with one another listening to the Alumni review old times with the
heart.-warming experiences, and to see so many in attendanc e is indeed
inspiring. A copy of the 1960 Masonic Home Newslette r No. 34 was
sent to all active Alumni and to Masonic Lodges currently sponsoring a
child in the Home, as well as to all Grand Lodge Officers.
The association with the children, the staff, and the magnitude of
friends of the Home continues to be richly rewarding . To the Craft and
to the various members of the Board of Trustees through these years. I
should again like to express my sincerest appreciati on for the confidence
and faith that has been tendered me in this joint service to the children of
our Brethren.

Respectfully submitted,
ROBERT M. HENRY, Superinte ndent

year to each Lodge which had not attained Merit Roll status. The names
of the Lodges also appeared in that issue.
Your Committee had some reservations when authorizing this action,
but actually was motivated by the request of many brethren visiting the
Temple. Since that publication, 32 additional Lodges have attained
Merit Roll status, and from the inquiries coming into the office, many
more Lodges are actively at work with Merit Roll status their goal.
This is most gratifying inasmuch as a recapitulation shows that if all
the non-Merit Roll Lodges reached this status, it would result in elimination of the $1 Per Capita Tax for all Lodges approximately two years
earlier than is now contemplated.
This is a Grand Lodge activity and every Lodge should want to
accomplish at least the minimum average of $10 per member. Many,
many have "trod the extra miles" and brought their averages up to far
in excess of the minimum.
The financing of the Temple is on a sound basis. Costs are known.
Payments to the banks are well in advance. At this writing it is more
important that every Lodge get its name on the Merit Roll than is the
amount of money involved (as important as this is) . When the debt is
finally paid, the opportunity to have the Lodge name inscribed on the
Bronze Plaque along with others who have done their rightful share
will have passed. The Merit Roll Plaque is a permanent part of the
building. It will continue to record the achievement of those Lodges who
have become "Builders of the Temple".

This is the Sixth Annual Report issued by the Board of Trustees of
the California Masonic Memorial Temple.
The Board of Trustees met following the close of the 1959 Annual
Communication of Grand Lodge, as is required by the By-Laws, for
the purpose of organization. The election of Brother Alfred F. Breslauer,
Deputy Grand Master; Brother Guy B. Mize, Senior Grand Warden;
and Brother Ira W. Coburn, Junior Grand Warden, was formally reported to the Board, and on motion duly made, seconded and carried,
they were elected members of the Board of Trustees. All officers were
re-elected to their respective offices.
The President also announced the appointment by the Grand Master
of new trustees John W. Davey and Rexford L. Hall to fill vacancies on
the Board for terms expiring in 1960 and 1961 respectively.
As a part of this report we have again included the Certified Public
Accountant's report, and the report of the Building Manager, Brother
Alvin A. Horwege. In addition to the capital expenditures as outlined in
the report of our manager, the screen to protect the endomosaic window
(referred to in our last annual report) has been installed.
OPEN BooK

Your Board of Trustees, through the cooperation of Kohnke Printing Company, has the Open Book on display in the entrance foyer. It is
contemplated that the original copy will be under security on the table
provided for that purpose. Pages will be turned from time to time. A
duplicate copy of all names is on file in the Grand Secretary's office, and
may be inspected by those interested in doing so.
MEMORIAL GIFTS

Provision has been made for the addition to the Open Book of the
names of those in whose memory gifts are made. Brother Washington
Kohnke has assured us that these names can be added at a later date.
CURRENT DONORS

Since the closing of the Open Book our staff has maintained a separate file of current donors. It is anticipated that some form of recognition
of these gifts will be made at a later date, or at any rate when the debt
is finally paid. Just what form such acknowledgment will take has not
been determined-it will depend on the number of names involved.

REPORT OF BUILDING MANAGE R
To the Trustees of California Masonic Memorial Temple:
Brethren:
In presenting this, my second annual report as manager of the California Masonic Memorial Temple, I express my pleasure for the cooperation and counsel of the Board of Trustees. who are ever alert in
eideavoring to place the operation of the Temple facilities in the best
light to the public. Two such examples are given below:
The ladies' rest room facilities (which were found inadequate) were
enlarged by eleven units:
The hydraulic ramp at our Pine Street loading dock (completed
during the year) has proved to be up to our fondest hopes. During sessions in the auditorium when we have about four hundred cars in the
garage. operation is put on a "park yourself' basis. A number of
attendants are stationed on the various floors, and at closing time
parkers may take the elevator directly to the floor on which they have
parked--dri ving their own cars out. The two lower decks are channeled
out to Pine Street without stop-using the hydraulic ramp. Since the
ramp has been in operation, we have never failed to empty the garage
in a maximum of thirty minutes. All who have used it are loud in their
expressions of approval.
During the year, the garage operation has reached a new high in
revenue, having grossed $41.347.24 in total income-an increase of
$6,269.06 over)ast year's revenue.
Our rental of the auditorium and exhibit space for the year covered
95 days of occupancy. Included in this occupancy were 58 days given
over to national and state conventions. It is estimated that attendance
during these 58 days amount to approximate ly 100,000 persons from all
over the United States. The other 37 were accounted for by shows, concerts, and church services, with an estimated combined attendance of
175.000.
With additional convention space becoming available in the hotels
of the city, we may expect heavy competition in this field during the
coming years. We are, however, receiving an increase in interest in our
auditorium for concerts and shows-for which it is ideally suited. While
convention competition promises to be heavy, the city's added facilities
are bound to increase the total business, and we may expect to share in
some of this increase.
In the interest of a better understandi ng of our facilities, and in order
to acquaint men in the convention and public relations field with what
we have to offer, we were host to two groups during the past year. The
San Francisco Covention & Visitors' Bureau directors, and the San Francisco Public Relations Forum were our guests at luncheons and tours of

100

our building on different occasions. President Siems outlined to these
men the many features of the auditorium and the exhibit Boor. One very
interesting use of our facilities was made by Westinghouse Electric
when they held their annual stockholders' meeting here.
A new brochure has been published-aimed at selling our facilities,
and plans are being made to place these in the hands of concert and convention managers.
Our guest register ihows that 4800 visitors signed the register. These
represent visitors from 47 states, and 36 foreign countries. Literally
thousands of visitors come to the Temple each year. Among them are
many distinguished in Masonry. We have had the pleasure this year
of having with us:

REPORT OF THE
MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT BOARD
This is the 28th Annual Report of the Masonic Homes Endowment
Board, covering the period of July 1, 1959 to June 30, 1960. A careful
and thoughtful study of the report will reveal many outstanding records
established by the Lodges during the past year.
PERCENTAGE OF PARTICIPATION
During the past year, cash contributions were received from 100,220
brethren throughout the Jurisdiction. This number compares with 93,425
individual contributions for the previous year for a net increase of 6,795
contributors. This number raised the "Percentage of Participation" from
39.2% the previous year to 41.4% this year. With the assistance of the
brethren we sincerely hope that this "Percentage of Participation" will
increase to at least 50% in the near future.
CASH CONTRIBUTIONS
Individual contributions through the Lodges this year totaled $551,150.34 for a net increase of $49,029.91 over the previous year. These
individual contributions through the Lodges do not include bequests,
memorials, special gifts, etc., which are shown on another page of this
report. Receipts from all sources to be added to the Endowment Fund
totaled $952, l 27. 49 for the fiscal year ending June 30, 1960.
HONOR ROLL LoDGES
This report lists 502 Lodges on the Honor Roll for 1960, as compared to 453 a year ago, for a net increase of 49 Honor Roll Lodges.
Unfortunately, some Lodges which were on the Honor Roll a year ago
did not maintain Honor Roll status for this year. However, it is encouraging to report that 54 Lodges attained the Honor Roll this year for the
very first time. Percentage-wise, 72% of the Lodges are now on the
Honor Roll whereas 5 years ago only 36% of the Lodges were enjoying
that distinction. These figures further demonstrate that "it can be done".
$3.00 OR MORE AVERAGE
Again, we give special recognition, congratulations and thanks to the
following 119 Lodges which not only attained the Honor Roll by an
average of $2.00 per member, but "went the second mile or more" by
sending in contributions averaging $3.00 or more per member:

Last year there were 79 Lodges in the above listing. This year there
are 119. To these 119 Lodges, the Honor Roll of $2.00 per member
average is but a stepping-sto ne or mile-post to a greater accomplishment, but not the ultimate goal. Again, our special congratulati ons and
thanks to these 119 Lodges for their outstanding accomplishment.
WILLS AND BEQUESTS

During the .fiscal year ending June 30, 1960, $174,167.38 was contributed to the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund through Bequests
left to this Fund by the Estates of those who have been called from
labor in this life. the .final and most lasting expression of their Masonic
love and affection. We hope all Masons may give serious thought to
this method of creating a loving and living Memorial by providng
a Bequest to the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund in their Will. Any
member of this Board will gladly furnish further information about this
important phase of our work and a special pamphlet is available which
gives much factual information on this subject. These pamphlets are also
available free to the Lodges for mailing to members.
PRINTED ITEMS

Again this year. the Homes Endowment Board has furnished more
than a million printed items, such as pamphlets, Stop-Think -Consolidat e
cards. Grand Master's Proclamations re Homes Endowment Month,
and various other printed forms, the items having been ordered by the
Lodges for mailing to members . .Jn addition, many Lodges have sent out
letters, post-cards, etc., to their members regarding contributions to the
Endowment Fund, and such items have been proven to be very effective
in stimulating contributions.
CHANGES IN ENDOWMEN T BOARD PERSONNEL

A year ago, the terms of Dr. Ernest G. Bashor, Norbert W. Mixter
and John W. Davey expired. Brother Bashor requested that he not be
reappointed for another term so he could devote more time to his many
other activities in professional, fraternal and social life. He had been
a member of this Board for nearly 25 years and was Chairman of the
Board for some 14 years. Those many years of service are self-evident
of his interest and devotion to this most worthy Masonic cause.
Brother Mixter requested that he not be reappointed to the Board
because of the pressure of business in his Drug Store which he owns
and operates in Exeter, California, and which made it increasingly difficult to devote the necessary time to the work of this Board.
Brother Davey was appointed by the Grand Master to serve on the
Board of Trustees of the California Masonic Memorial Temple in lieu
of another term on the Endowment Board. He replaced John M. Gordon

104

on the Temple Board, who had been serving on both Boards for a
number of years but who resigned from the Temple Board in order to
devote more time to the Homes Endowment Board.
Our sincere thanks go to Brothers Bashor, Mixter and Davey for
the many years of service they devoted to this work and though their
activity on the Board ceases we know that their interest in the Homes
and the Endowment Board will continue for a long time to come.
To fill the vacancies on this Board left by these three members,
M. W. Joe L. Shell, Grand Master, appointed Brother Fred H. Blanchard of Los Angeles, Brother Harold R. DeTuncq of Arvin, California,
and Brother Howard L. Rose of Turlock, California, each to serve a
term of three years on the Homes Endowment Board. They assumed
their new duties in October of 1959 and have been working diligently
in their respective localities for the interests of the Endowment Board.

Our special thanks to the Masters, Wardens and other Lodge
Officers, and to the Lodge Endowment committees for their untiring
efforts and interest and in their pride in wanting to accomplish a fine
record for their Lodge and for the Homes Endowment program.
Last, but not least, our sincere thanks to the more than 100,000
brethren who made a contribution of their financial means that others less
fortunate might continue to have a home and loving care.

OuR THANKS To ALL

As usual, it is impossible to appropriately and adequately thank the
hundreds of brethren who had a part in the work of the Homes Endowment during the past year. Our special thanks go to the Grand Master,
M. W. Joe Shell, for his untiring assistance and for his so kindly mentioning the Homes and the Endowment in all of his talks to Masonic
Meetings, as well as the courtesies and encouragement he extended
to the Members of the Board in general and to its Chairman in particular. Likewise, our thanks and appreciation to the other Grand Lodge
Officers and Past Grand Masters; To Brother Don G. Campbell, Grand
Lecturer, and his corps of Assistant Grand Lecturers and Inspectors, all
of whom have given so freely of their time and efforts to encourage and
assist in our work, and without whose assistance we could not have
established the fine records which are shown elsewhere in this Report.
Again, the Secretaries of the Lodges have done an outstanding job
for the Homes Endowment and we wish we could find some method of
adequately thanking them. It is they who usually order and send out
the printed material furnished by this Board as well as letters and cards
written by the Secretaries to their members. Also, they are the ones who
do the work of receiving the contributions, issuing receipts, keeping the
records of contributions and remitting the funds to the Grand Secretary.
In many Lodges, we feel that the success of the Endowment program
rests with the Secretary.
In addition to the Lodge Secretaries, we give special thanks to the
Grand Secretary, M. W. Lloyd E. Wilson: the Assistant Grand Secretary, Henry D. Oliphant, and their entire office staff, all of whom are
always so willing to assist the members of this Board and who cooperate
100% at all times.

REPORT OF BOARD OF CONTROL
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. 6 A. M. of California:
The Board of Control submitts herewith its annual report covering
pertinent data on the activities of our Boards of Relief and their Employment Bureaus.
We are pleast;d to report that the work being carried on by our Executive Secretaries and employees continues to reflect credit and honor
on our ancient Institution. These devoted brethren and their employees
continue to go far beyond the call of duty, on foot and out of their way,
in carrying out their work. The Board of Control appreciates, as we are
sure this Grand Lodge does. their unselfish devotion and dedication to
their duties. No money can buy that kind of devotion, brethren; it can
only be acquired by the application of the tenets of Freemasonry to the
hearts of men.
We now have in our Jurisdiction nineteen Boards of Relief, five of
which operate Employment Bureaus. During the past year one new
Board of Relief has been organized in Orange County consisting, originally, of ten Lodges. These Lodges and their brethren have embarked
upon their new undertaking with an enthusiasm and determination
which can only bode a long and successful association together.
The activities of all of our Boards of Relief are supervised by the
Board of Control, directly. Uniform standards have been established
for operations, reporting, and auditing, by which we are able to keep
a watchful eye upon all of the operations for which we are responsible.
The Board of Control holds at least three meetings each year at
which times we meet with our Board of Relief Secretaries in order that

122

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

we may have a more personal contact with them and they with each
other, and that we all may have a better understanding of our respective
problems and responsibilities.

Of course, our Employment Bureaus operate without charge. If fees
for our services had been charged on the basis of rates fixed for comsnercial agencies, such employment opportunities would have cost our
Masonic family $101,973.14. In other words, our Fraternity has actually
saved over $100,000.00 by using our facilities.

After carefully analyzing the audited reports which have been submitted by our nineteen Boards of Relief. we ask your brief indulgence
in the following condensed statistics covering their operations during
the Masonic Year ended June 30, 1960:
Advanced for RelieL ................................. $40,690.18
Funerals conducted .............................................. 1,022
Total calls made-............................... - ...............29,780
Calls on the sick. ...........................•................... -9,772
Investigations conducted...................................... 2,212
Relief calls made..................................................8,043
Miscellaneous calls made....................................9,753
Obviously, these activities cannot be carried on without untiring
and dedicated devotion and work, much of it necessary after the hours
when most of us have locked our desks for the night. These heroic
Masons deserve and should have the undying gratitude of the entire
Craft.
BLOOD BANKS

Many of our Boards of Relief operate Masonic Blood Banks, and
those which do not usually have some other provision for providing
blood to Masons or their dependents when necessary. The following
figures indicate the extent of our blood donation activities during the
past year:
Units of blood donated........................................ 3, 491
Units of blood withdrawn ....................................3,403
Actual cost saved to our Masonic family ........ $84,185
EMPLOYMENT BUREAUS

As stated above, we now have Employment Bureaus within five of
our Boards of Relief. Their purpose, of course, is to assist our Masonic
family to obtain gainful employment. The increasing competition of our
public placement agencies in this field, as well as other factors, has occasioned a rapid decline in our placements over the years. and a corresponding rise in the cost of each placement. The Board of Control
has been keeping a concerned and watchful eye on this trend for a
number of years with the fear that if it continued, there might somewhere come a time when the results in this field might not justify their
cost. The following figures briefly cover the operations of our Employment Bureaus during the past Masonic Year:
Registered for employment.................................. 6,184
Positions actually secured.................................. 1, 161

REINBtJRSEMENTS TO MASONIC BoARDS OF RELIEF

It has long been the policy of this Grand Lodge that no worthy
sojourning brother, or his immediate family. shall suffer in our Jurisdiction for the necessities of life, or shall have other than a decent burial
upon their demise, regardless of the willingness.or ability of the brother's
own Lodge to make us whole. Grand Lodge undertakes to reimburse
any Board of Relief for such unrecoverable advances. During the past
Masonic Year our Boards of Relief advanced more than $40,000.00
to sojourners and their dependents. All such advances were carefully
scrutinized by one of our Executive Secretaries and efforts were made
to obtain reimbursement from the sojourner's home Lodge. It is gratifying to report that out of $40,690.18 advanced during the year, only
$577.01 was not repaid, in accordance with the following requests to
Grand Lodge for reimbursement:
REIMBURSEMENTS TO THE SAN FRANCISCO BOARD OF RELIEF

covers two cases. One is a continuing case over many years of a very
worthy brother from Scotland for whom the Grand Lodge of Scotland
makes some provision, but not sufficient for his essential needs. The

To the Most Worship ful Grand Lodge F. 8 A. M. of California:
Your Committee on Commercialism is indeed happy to advise that
reported violations of our law are diminishing in number, scope and
seriousness. Obviously, as you will note from that which follows, continued vigilance is necessar y to prevent the taint of Commercialism from
again rearing its ugly head in our midst.
SHRINE

This Appenda nt Organiza tion generally has been most cooperative.
The several football games which they sponsor, also a basketba ll game
in Hawaii have been handled strictly in line with Grand Lodge's requirements. We have had discussions with Imperial Potentat e Andrews ,
relative to their activities in this jurisdiction, and have his assuranc e
that our law will be strictly observed . We must report, however , there
have been two instance s where Shrine Clubs, one in the southern part
of the state and the other in the north, violated our law. Both violations
were called to the attention of our M . W. Grand Master. His prompt
action in regard thereto has, we are sure, satisfact orily disposed of these
situations.
Early in June this year there was held in San Francisc o a Pollack
Bros. "Shrine" Circus sponsore d by the Knights of Columbus. Obviously, the use of the word "Shrine" in connection with this circus
has good advertisi ng value. Our Grand Master wrote the Imperial
Potentate . This resulted in a letter from the Imperial Recorde r dated
August 2 at the instance of the Imperial Potentat e to the manager of
Pollack Bros. Circus stating that any such future violations would place
his, Stern's, and others in his organiza tion who were Shriners , membership in the Shrine in jeopardy. In his response of August 9, Mr. Stern
admits the error stating it was made inadvert ently by the printer of
the tickets and assured the Imperial Potentat e that it would not be
repeated.

At this time our greatest problem is the attempt by Publishe rs of
certain Eastern Magazin es, apparent ly centralized in Chicago to sell,
by high pressure long distance phone, advertisi ng in their magazine,
basing their call on the fact that it is an official Masonic Publication.
The Grand Lodge of Illinois is greatly distressed as result of these
activities and is moving to eliminate this continuing source of trouble.
We are combatting this situation as much as is possible and in a manner
which should not place this Grand Lodge in jeopardy .
Recently we were informed of two men who called on a Service Station Man - not a member of the Craft, in Redding . Californ ia. They
approach ed him as follows: "We are with the Freemas on Magazin e.
You have several members dealing with you and, since you do not pay
dues to the Lodge, these members feel you should take out a good ad
in their magazine, so we have put you down for $100.00. This magazine,
with your ad, will be distribut ed free to each member from all over the
State that attends this Grand 1Lodge Convent ion here in Redding ." It
so happene d that a member of the Craft, known to the Service Station
People, arrived on the scene at this time. This Brother ran the salesmen
off the premises. He also contacte d one of the local Judges who sent him
to the District Attorney , who in turn sent him to the Chief of Police.
With the Chief of Detectiv es this Brother went to the hotel where they
talked to both men, looked at their Sales Book, after which they were
placed under arrest. In their attempt to arrange bail, they exposed their
headqua rters in Portland . Oregon.
Additionally, we have had called to our attention several instances
of solicitation for advertisi ng by salesmen of Masons and non~Masons
for a magazine call "Freema son," presuma bly the same publication

"M1scEL LANEOu s"

"Brother Henders on" represen ting a Life Insuranc e Compan y using
radio broadcas ts in attempti ng to secure clients. This man's card carried
a Masonic Emblem, the Square and Compass . It was found that he
apparent ly is an irregular Mason. He was contacte d, and the .Pr?blem
has been solved by his assuranc e that the Emblem has been ehmmate d
and will not be used.
One nationall y organize d firm wrote for authority to manufac ture
a steel tape rule carrying a Masonic Emblem and called attention to
cigarette lighters, desk sets, etc. marked in this manner. We advised
them that our name and emblem were registere d under the Californ ia
Corporat ion Code, and the unauthor ized use was prohibite d for which
reason the authority requeste d could not be granted. An Eastern
manufac turer wrote to the Secretar y of some of our Lodges. enclosing
a reflector emblem to be placed on automobiles. and in this manner
tndeavor ed to sell the Lodge on the idea of raising funds by selling

of the Californ ia Law referred to in the precedin g item and requeste d
them to desist from their activities. Further. that any orders received
would not be filled and any checks received would be returned with
latisfact ory explanat ion. There have been some other matters called
to our attention , none of which is of particula rly great importance and
so will not be commented on. Suffice it to say that either by word of
mouth or by letter all such matters have been successfully concluded
in accordance with requirem ents of our law.
We have had called to our attention an item which appeared in a

Order of Caritas, which is forbidden under Grand Lodge edict adopted
in 1957. In replying to our Grand Master's letter concerning this,
the Brother stated that the news item was in error as his resignati on had
been tendered in compliance with Grand Lodge edict of 1957.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. 6 A. M. of California:
The Investment Committee concludes its tenth year of activity, and
herewith renders its report for the twelve months ending June 30, 1960.
Each year's report gives a certain amount of historical background and
basic information, which should be helpful to those attending Grand
Lodge for the first time.
The Prudent Man Rule in modified form was adopted by Grand
Lodge at its 1950 Communication. For the Constituent Lodges a Prudent Man Rule was adopted :in 1951.
The Investment Committee of Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California
was formed for the purpose of administering the investable funds of
Grand Lodge, the Masonic Homes of California, and the Masonic
Homes Endowment Fund. The Committee does not supervise the investments of Constituent Lodges. Grand Lodge makes the services of its
investment advisor available to the Lodges. Many Lodges are now making use of this service, as evidenced by the fact that 245 Lodges with over
$5,000,000 of investments are now consulting with our investment advisor.
The Investment Committee is composed of the Grand Treasurer,
the Assistant ·Grand Treasurer, the Chairman of the Finance Committee,
the President of the Masonic Homes Board of Trustees or a Trustee of
that Board designated by him, and the Chairman of the Masonic Homes
Endowment Board or a member of that Board designated by him. Past
Grand Master Charles M. Wollenberg, former President of the Masonic
Homes Board of Trustees, had appointed Brother Past Master Ralph H.
Head as his representative. Henceforth, the new President of the Board
of Trustees, Past Grand Master Arthur M. Warren by virtue of his
office will personally serve as a member of the Committee. John M .
Gordon, Chairman of the Endowment Board, also serves as a member
of the Committee.
By Ordinance, under .Section 246 ( formerly 86) with respect to investment of Grand Lodge funds, and Section 403 (formerly 152.1)
respecting investments by Constituent Lodges, the following provisions
prevailed as of June 30, 1960:
GROUP I. At least 20% of the funds available for investment
must be in:

130

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

A) Cash and/or bank accounts.
B) Obligations of the United States.
C) Obligations of the State of California and its political subdivisions.
D) Such other securities as are legal invesments for savings
banks in California or Hawaii (As amended 1959).
GROUP II. Up to 20% may be invested in:
A) Other evidences of indebtedness, which are or will be fully
listed and registered on an Exchange registered with the
Securities and Exchange Commission as a National Securities Exchange, except that this listing requirement shall not
include railroad equipment trust issues ( 1955.).
B) Preferred stocks, which are or will be fully listed and registered on an exchange registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission as a National Securities Exchange, except that full listing and registration of preferred stock shall
not be required whenever the common stock of the corporation issuing such preferred stock is fully listed and registered
on such an exchange, provided that such preferred stock is
traded on such an exchange ( 1956).
GROUP UL Up to 60% may be invested in:
A) Common stocks, which must be fully listed and registered
on an exchange registered with the Securities and Exchange
Commission as a National Securities Exchange, except that
this listing requirement shall not apply to bank and insurance
stocks.
B) Shares of Investment Trusts.
C) Shares and/or certificates of insured Federal or State Savings
and Loan Associations ( 1957 and 1959). The amount invested in any one Association shall not exceed the amount
covered by insurance.
(THIS AMENDMENT APPLIES ONLY TO CONSTITUENT LODGES AND DOES NOT APPLY TO
THE INVESTMENT OF GRAND LODGE FUNDS.)
With respect to the authority to invest in Groups II and Ill. the
Ordinances read as follows: "No such investments, however, shall be
made which at the time of purchase will result in the total market value
of the securities referred to in this section exceeding twenty per cent
(or sixty per cent) of the total market value of all the cash, bank accounts
and securities held,"-the controlling point being that there cannot be

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

inore than 20% or 60% invested in Groups II and HI. respectively, at
the time of purchase.
Should a Lodge elect to invest its funds under the provisions of
Group II or Ill hereof. it shall confer and counsel as to any such propased or contemplated investments with the professional Investment
Advisor used by Grand Lodge, whose fees will be paid by Grand Lodge.
At the 1959 Communication certain amendments were passed with
respect to the percentages which could be invested in Groups I and III.
Group I was reduced to 20% and Group III was increased to 60%. In
this connection, it is very important to call attention to the following,
which is contained in the Reports of the Committee on Jurisprudence
and the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
"Your Committee on Jurisprudence respectfully calls attention to
the fact that this proposed amendment is permissive only and is not a
directive. Great care should be exercised in making investments under
the authority granted by this pr~osed amendment."
"Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends the
adoption of Resolution D-7 but with this admonition to the Lodges:
"A) The authority granted is permissive only and is not suggested
as an investment guide under present economic conditions.
"B) That in making investments in Group III the Lodge be most
circumspect in taking advantage of this additional authority.
"C) And that they strictly comply with the provisions of the last
paragraph of Section 403-3B of our ordinances, consult with and heed
the advice of the professional investment advisors used by Grand Lodge,
and made available to the Constituent Lodges without charge to the
individual Lodge."
The above comments are included in the reports of the Committees
as they appear on page 282 of the 1959 Proceedings.
Since its formation the Investment Committee has met regularly every
three months. Between quarterly meetings the business of the Committee
is handled by correspondence or telephone.
As stated, we have just completed ten years of operation. The following is a summary of the consolidated market value of securities
owned, plus investable cash, together with a record of dollar income on
these investments, beginning with November 30, 1950, and for each
aucceeding fiscal year, through June 30, 1960, including the percentage
income on the market value of each year.

In the fiscal year 1959-1960 there was liquidated from the Masonic
Homes General Fund and Flint Fund securities to the extent of $1.109,000, and in the previous year to the extent of $106,000 (or a total of
$1,215,000) , in order to pay for the new hospital and facilities at Decoto.
The hospital was dedicated on July 30, 1960, and the total cost was approximately $1,300,000.
We have had practically one hundred per cent attendance at our
Investment Committee meetings. P. G. M. Arthur M. Warren attended
the November 1959 and February and ,May 1960 meetings, as a member
of the Board and later President of Masonic Homes Board of Trustees.
The entire portfolio is listed in the Auditor's Reports and is, therefore, not included herein. The securities are held in safekeeping by the
Trust Department of the Crocker Anglo National Bank, at its One
Montgomery Street Office, San Francisco.
With respect to Constituent Lodges, Moody's reports that the latest
record indicates a total of 245 Lodges making use of their service, which
is an increase of 19 over a year ago. The Committee was pleased to note
that some of the Lodges are making good and continuing use of the
service. The varying size of the investment portfolios would of course
have a bearing on the activities of the Lodges. A calculated total would
indicate that the funds reviewed are well in excess of $5,000,000. The
reviews are completely up to date and have been so maintained. The contact with the Lodges is carried out on a continuing basis, thereby indicating that the service rendered to the Lodges, both by Grand Lodge and
its Investment Advisor, has been very useful.
The Hawaiian Lodges have a resolution to present respecting Hawaiian securities and the listing thereof, with which the Committee
agrees.
The Committee endeavors to keep in as close touch with economic

135

conditions as is humanly possible. These are ever changing. Now we
are confronted with different factors , and the law of supply and demand
is again operating. Increased costs of doing business cannot be passed
along as in recent years. Therefore, competition again gets into full
swing and the margin of profits declines. This competition comes not
only within the United States, but from all over the world. How quickly
things change-a year ago the Investment Committee asked for a change
in percentages, which was done for protection against inflation, should
it become more rampant. Fortunately. it was not necessary to use this
authority, inasmuch as the inflationary forces were held in check. Instead,
the Investment Committe has become more conservative, as exhibited by
the fact that we have less invested in Group III than we did a year ago.
But we now have the authority to be more flexible if need be.
Let it also be mentioned that our course of action can be quite different from that of an individual investor. This is said so as not to influence
you with respect to your personal actions.
The Investment Committee, to repeat, continues to pursue a conservative policy, as evidenced by the fact that we have 53.83% invested in
Group I. 17.67% in Group II, and only 28.50% in Group III, of which
11 %% is in industrial stocks, the balance being in finance and utility
stocks.
Our thanks to the Grand Secretary, the Assistant Grand Secretary,
and my thanks to the members of the tl nvestment Committee for their
wholehearted and generous cooperation at all times.

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON
OLD MASONIC HALL AT LOS ANGELES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
Reference is made to previous reports of this committee for information on this first Masonic Hall in Los Angeles.
Under the direction of Brother Orvel B. Johnson, Direct Construction Supervisor for the State, the work of restoration of this Hall is
proceeding rapidly, with a schedule of completion in 1961.
The State of California, owner of El Pueblo de Los Angeles State
Historical Monument, of which this old Masonic Hall is a part, has
entered into a franchise agreement with the City of Los Angeles under
which the City will be the operators of the Monument. A lease is in
preparation between the State and the City on one hand and the
Grand Lodge of California under which the second floor Lodge room
of the Hall will be leased to Grand Lodge for a term of years at nominal
rental. The form and terms of this lease will conform in all basic respects
to that which exists between the State and Grand Lodge on the Columbia
Temple. It was not possible to have the lease in shape for approval by
Grand Lodge at this Communication, but it should be ready within the
next ninety days. Because the Hall may be ready for occupancy before
Grand Lodge convenes in 1961, this Committee recommends that authority now be given to the proper officers of Grand Lodge to execute
this lease as submitted in final form.
We, therefore, offer the following resolution:
"RESOLVED, that the proper officers of Grand Lodge are
hereby authorized and empowered to execute a lease on the Old
Masonic Hall at 416 North Main Street, Los Angeles."
You will be pleased to know that in the entire program for the preservation and restoration of this Masonic Landmark, which has covered the
last eight years, Grand Lodge has not been involved in any expense.
Nor do we anticipate any until we occupy the second floor Lodge room
and furnish jt. We have been informed that Los Angeles Lodge No. 42,
which first occupied the Hall in 1858, will underwrite that expense.
We recommend the continuation of a Special Committee and the
authority, previously granted, for the Grand Master to make nominal
expenditures, if necessary.
Respectfully submitted,
FRANK HARWELL, JR.
MATIHEW M. CODON
GuYB.M1zE
Resolution and entire report unanimously adopted.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON PUBLIC SCHOOLS
To the Most Worship{ ul Grand Lodge F. & A. M . of California:

I. PREFACE
This preface to this 1960 report for the Public Schools Committee
must do one thing with real zest. That one thing is to thank those who,
with dedication, devotion, conviction, and clear concepts, gave the
Grand Lodge Public Schools activity during 1960 its greatest year.
To our Grand Master, Most Worshipful Joe L. Shell. to the officers
and the staff members in Grand Lodge hea dquarters go our first and
greatest expression of thanks. The Grand Lodge influence throughout
the family of Masonic Lodges and the related bodies in California is
the spark which stimulates the zeal with which those who serve the
Public Schools Committee program are fired. 1960 has been a year of
extra effort on the part of Masons in their loyalty and faithfulness,
helping to extend the ideals and sustain the personnel in every position
and relationship to Public Schools in California.
The good feeling, the success and the results accomplished in California Public Schools a re the awa rds and rewards for Masonic support
for Public Education.
We thank Lodge Officers and Committeemen in each Blue Lodge
in California for their excellent efforts. Appreciation is extended to
every state and local community organization, group, and agency which
rallied to the call tha t was expressed up and down California to strive
for the best for Public Education.
Results were achieved worthy of the efforts extended. The program
of public interest in and loyalty to Public Education in the areas of
influence of the Grand Lodge of California have been noteworthy in
our two states, California and Hawaii.
To those who worked, who followed the directions of our Grand

To those who have prepared, brought. and displayed their exhibits
- a special word of compliment and commendation. It is you who
demonstrate the "know-How" - you prove that results are a ttained,
that "work" will do the job. Thank to you.

IL THE PURPOSES GUIDIN G THE PUBLIC SCHOOLS COMMITTEE 1960
Our purposes for the 1960 activities thro ughout the entire year in
every Lodge in California and Hawaii centered in the 1960 theme " Our Public Schools - Know Them - Support Them - Strengthen
Them."
When we speak of "Knowing the Public Schools" we refer not
solely to the physical plants, the personnel. and the students. We refer
to the basic principles which are the foundation for Public Education
in our country, in its several states . and even in its various communities.
We are firm in our belief that a true principle of Masonic expression in
practical living in our society has unceasingly bound our fraternit.y
to the ideals. the operation. the strength, and the advancement of Pubhc
Education, Public Schools, public school teachers and teaching.
1960 has been a year of study and presenta tion of the histor y of
Public Education in our States of California and Hawaii.
We have emphasized the importance of. the ve ry indispensability
of good Public Education in the American system of gov~rn m~~t in
the United States. It is a basic truth that knowledge of the why and
the "how" of Public Education is a foundation for the security of Public
Education, the security of the understanding of the meaning of F reedom as we know it, and of its preservation.
It has been a vigorous purpose, which 1960 efforts have served, to
keep the members of all phases of Masonic life within Blue Lodges,
within related Masonic bodies . in the family and households of M asons
and their friends, informed, alert, active, and united in behalf of better
Public Schools, better, happier, and more secure public school teachers.
We have adhered to the purpose tha t our fraternity must not stand
alone in support of the ideals and safety of our Public Schools a~d
Public Education. We have worked with and have been supported m
staunch fas hion by such faithful and loyal interpreters of the public
schools as The California Teachers Association, The California Congress of Parents and Teachers, Churches of many faiths. all groups
of organized labor. every Veterans organization, professions related. to
public education, such as Welfare bodies, Playground and Recreati.on
agencies, Health societies, all media of ~ommunication and cultural mterests in every community. The Womens groups th roughout our states

as well as Business. Professional. and Chamber of Commerce organizations have taken and given strength to the cause of Public Education
and our Public Schools. This purpose is one of our finest.
Another purpose which has advanced the cause of our responsibility
to Public Education is that of having each Lodge draw closer to local
Public Schools as institutions which serve the ideals of Americanism as
does no other agency. Our purpose of having each Lodge have a Public
Schools Committee to act as an alert body of M asonic Brethren in the
Lodge who will present reports. information, literature; offer discussions and s uggestions in matters is a vigorous. valiant. and succesful
purpose. In a constructive and welcome manner such committees keep
all members of the fraternity in close touch with Public Schools. Our
Public Schools become crentures of society into which Masons have
always desired that the Public Schools add greatest ideals and strength.
A great purpose which Grand Lodge Committee on Public Schools
has served to advance during 1960 is the proposition that each and every
Mason know of the beginnings of Public Education in the United
States of America. That every Masonic citizen know the reasons why
there is no possible substitute for Public Schools in our way of life.

The many publications which in recent months have issued from
the several bodies of the Masonic Fraternity have constituted valuable
materials which local Lodge Public Schools C ommittees could present
and discuss with Lodge membership. S uch ma terial has been of great

Education materials which are of extraordinary appeal and interest are
available for brie f showings and discussions in Lodges. All this to make
more vivid the valuable support for Public Schools as Masonic loyalties
to Public Education would stress.
M any times Public Schools Committee material has taken written
form in the official organ of the Lodge. Many inspired speakers have
gone to school and community sessions with an expression of good
will, friendship, and confidence in public schools and their personnel.
This has been no political. personal. or self-seeking expression. It is in
the realm of faith in our country as attained through Public Education. We herein manifest our faith in youth a nd serve to inspire them
to complete their education.
Throughout the year service has been rendered by the Public Schools
Committee in the building up of public rebtions con tacts for P ublic
Schools. More than 300 speeches and talks have been given to Teachers
Institute sessions, Parent Teacher Associa tion. Service Club. and other
community groups on the theme "Good Public Education. Indispensable
in a Democracy." Background and basic principles for such presentations are found in and well supported by Masonic lessons. These contacts have been made by the Grand Lodge Public Schools Committee
in one year.
We have carried to the youth of our schools the fundamental meanings of good education and better learning as a n objective which they
as young citizens should accept.
The annual publication of the Grand Lodge Committee was more
popular and in greater demand during 1960 than ever before. There
were more requests for the copies to be supplied after they were d istributed than were available in the original printing.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON MASONIC HISTORY
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
Your Committee is pleased to see the continued interest in the illustrated lecture of old. pioneer Lodges, entitled "SOME CAME BY
LAND AND SOME CAME BY SEA," which is still being shown
among the Lodges. Although engagements have tapered off somewhat
from I 958-59, requests continue to come in. As an example, three showings are scheduled for this coming month of October. Although we ~till
feel that the greatest benefit will be derived when Lodges and districts
join together in their requests for a showing, we are willing to appear
before individual Lodges.
Requests for dates should be addressed to the Chairman, Grand
Lodge Committee on Masonic History. To facilitate assignment of dates,
please submit a choice of three dates with your request and, if your
Lodge is located more than an hour's drive from the Bay Area or from
Los Angeles. then you should select a Friday or a Saturday evening
as our lecturers generally are unable to accept mid-week engagements.
If you cannot secure your Lodge Hall on a Friday or Saturday evening .
say so in your request, indicating the evenings when the Hall will be
a vailable, and the Committee will make every effort to accommodate you.

It has been proposed that the following letter from the History
Committee be sent to the Worshipful Masters of the several Lodges in
California, to-wit:
Dear Worshipful Master and Brothers:
In order to bring the history of Freemasonry in California up to
date, the History Committee has been assigned the pleasant duty of
preparing the complete history of Freemasonry in California for the
ten year period from 1950 through 1960.
This history is to include the following events which have taken
place in your Lodge within the ten year period above stated:
I. Observance of a Centennial and other Anniversaries, including
the entire programs thereof.
2. Lodge dedication.
3. Cornerstone laying.
4. Formation of a Lodge made up of members from your old Lodge.
5. New Temple.
6. Mortgage burning.
7. Unusual and distinctive events and unusual happenings in the
history of your Lodge and its members .
If there is any doubt in your mind as to the advisability of including
any additional information not enumerated in the above categories. feel
free to send same. It may be that we have failed tci include facts highly
essential to our main objective.
Will the present Master kindly undertake the task of assembling
the above facts. If for any reason the present Master finds it inconvenient, or does not desire to identify himself with this work, will he
please appoint some competent member of the Lodge who will assist
us in the compilation of this work, and forward the name and address
to the undersigned at the above address. We suggest that the person
designated be given the title of "Lodge Historian," and that he send
preliminary material as soon as possible so that the work of sorting and
organizing may begin.
Fraternally,
LEON 0. WHITSELL. Chairman

We respectfully request that the sum of $3,000.00 be appropriated
for our use for the ensuing year.

REPORT OF
SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON DE MOLAY
To the M ost Worshipful Grand Lodge F. 6 A. M. of California:
Your Committee on DeMolay has just concluded a most interesting
and rewarding year. We are pleased to submit the following report to
you for your approval. There is a continuing active interest in the
sponsorship of DeMolay Chapters by constituent Lodges. With reports
from only two-thirds of t he State of California, we have confirmation
of I 09 Lodges sponsoring Chapters of the Order of DeMolay. The list
attached to this report records those Lodges that have assumed sponsorship during the Masonic Year just concluded.
This Committee has received complete cooperation from DeMolay
leadership. As a result . the policies of this Grand Lodge ha ve been
unequivocally accepted. In fact. we have been called upon many times
to address groups of DeMolays and their Advisors on the subjects of
Masonic regulations and customs. There have been no reports during
the past year of any actions by DeMolay Chapters, inadvertent or
otherwise, which were not consistent with Grand Lodge policies.
That there is a marked increase in Masonic interest in DeMolay is
evident by the number of requests that we have received to speak on
the subject before Lodges. District Officers' Meetings and Masonic
Groups of all kinds. One of our cherished memories of this past year
was the reception given to a talk on DeMolay delivered to a dinner
meeting sponsored by the Southern California Research Lodge prior
to one of their well attended popular seminars .
Many outstanding activities were observed by your Committee. These
included the Annual DeMolay Week Observance by the Sa n Diego
County Masonic Officers' Association, the Bright Side of Youth program in Oakland. DeMolny Days at the State and Los Angeles County
Fairs. State and Jurisdictional Conventions, workshops and a host of
public ceremonies. Every activity was conducted in such a manner as to
win the praise of the communities involved . Masonry can be very proud
of the accolades earned by them. Whether it is by our choosing or not.
the average citizen has come to regard DeMolay as the product of
Masonry. We should be grateful that this rega rd has reflected credit
upon us. and we should do everything in our power to insure the continuation of the outstanding record being compiled by the Order of
DeMolay.
We were surprised to find that a portion of our membership does
not have an understanding of the Order of DeMolay. In some instances
we noted considerable misinformation on the subject. This has prompted
the committee to begin compiling material for an informational brochure
on DeMolay. We had hoped to have this task completed by the time
that this report was prepared. However, there is still some work that

148

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

needs to be done and we commend the completion of this project to the
committee that may be appointed for next year.
Our Grand Master has been most generous in his support and encouragement of the work of this committee. We wish to express to him
our most sincere thanks and appreciation.
It is our recommendation that this committee be continued and that
the sum of $750.00 be appropriated to cover its necessary expenses.
In closing, let us remember what the poet has written, "Who touches
a boy. by the Master's Plan, shapes the course of the future man ."
Respectfully submitted.

The Committee on Lodge Financing respectfully submits its report
of the transactions of the several Lodges and Temple Associations operating Temple properties within the jurisdiction, together with a brief
comparison of the las t two years financial status of the operation of the
properties which shows considerable improvement for the I 959-1960
Masonic year.
During the past year the Committee on Lodge Financing has assisted
in and has approved the formation of seventeen ( 17 ) new Masonic
Temple Associations which were incorporated as non-profit corporations under the Laws of the state of California; has approved the purchase of seven ( 7) new building sites for Masonic Temples; has approved the purchase of five ( 5) existing buildings which were found
to be suitable for use as Masonic Ti!mples; has approved seven ( 7) applications for consent to commence construction of new Masonic Temples; and has approved eighteen ( 18) applications for consent to make
capital improvements in existing Masonic Temples. The above are only
the major items of business conducted by the Committee. Many other
transactions were made which are far too numerous to report.
For the past three ( 3) years. the Committee has carried on a vigorous campaign to assist the Brethren operating Temples in improving
financial operations. This included assisting the Brethren to secure
adequate rental for use of the Temples, assistance in financial improvement, help in methods of proper financial accounting, and the setting up
of adequate cash reserves for future obligations and depreciation. The
Brethren have cooperated fully with the Committee and exemplary
results have been achieved. The report of the Committee at the meeting of Grand Lodge in September. 1959 showed great improvement in
the financial status of the Temple Associations. This past year, the
Brethren have really taken over and have made even greater improvement. The results of operations for the past year are astounding.
The following comparison of the past two years of operation will
more graphically show the specific improvement:

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON RITUAL
( B-1)

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
This resolution, presented by the Master. Wardens and certain
Past Masters of Lynwood Lodge No. 600, proposes to substitute for the
singing of the national hymn "America," the singing of the national
anthem, in connection with the retirement of the Flag.
The Masonic ceremony of presenting and of retiring the Flag is
not a public ceremony; it is strictly a private and Masonic one, performed only in a tiled lodge. We do not attempt to conform to the
requirements of a public Flag ceremony.
When the Flag is presented, under our adopted ceremony. only the
Pledge of Allegiance is given. It is only in the retirement of the Flag
that any verse is sung. At such time, in retiring the Flag . this Committee
feel s that the national hymn-actually a prayer for Divine protection
of our Country- is more appropriate than the anthem. It has been used
in our Flag ceremonies for 30 years.
Very few of the members of any lodge can carry the high range
required for the national anthem. without music or the assistance of
trained voices. Consequently. the use of the verse of "America" is much
more practical.
However, in view of the earnest desire of some lodge to use " The
Star Spangled Banner" instead of " America," we propose the following resolution:
RESOLVED. that the Monitor and Officers' Manual be amended
at page 56 thereof to delete the paragraph reading as follows: "The
~.faster then says: 'The Brethren will join in singing one verse of
~m~ric~".'.(One verse of "America" should then be sung.), by substitutmg m heu thereof the following:
"The M aster then says: 'The Brethren will join in singing

164

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORN IA

one verse of " America"' (or) 'The Brethren will join in singing
one verse of "The Star Spangled Banner".' (The verse is then
sung.) (The verse of "The Star Spangled Banner" should be
sung only where there is musical accompaniment.)
Respectfully submitted,

GRAND ORATION
"THE SPIRIT OF FREEMASONRY IN A
TIME THAT TRIES MEN'S SOU LS"
JuDGE GERALDS. LEVIN, GRAND ORATOR

Tribute to Grand Master
"Render therefore to all their dues: tribute to
whom tribute is due; * * * honour to whom honour."
-ROMAN S C. 13, V. 7.
It seems appropriate, not simply because of my gratitude to the
Grand Master for the opportunity to serve the Grand Lodge of California as Grand Orator but principally because of his characte r a nd
outstanding contribution to Freemasonry. that before launching into the
Grand Oration I should pay tribute in the presence of this honorable
and illustrious company to a great Mason. our Grand Master, Joe L.
Shell. I know you will forgive me for taking advantage of this appearance to do so. I believe my remarks may be given some measure of
credence, since they are based on my observation of the Grand M aster
in action in many parts of this State through a most interesting a nd
challenging Masonic year.
Our Grand Master, affectionately known by thousands of M asons
as just plain "Joe", is decidely a personality that no robes or insignia of
office can bemask. His individuality is so strong that he is incapable o f
masquerading or a ssuming a role other than the real part he plays in
daily life. His every thought and action has been mellowed by gentleness,
humility of spirit and purity of soul. No prejudices. no desire for popular
acclaim, no unworthy motive has distorted his judgment. He has been
guided by wisdom and an abiding passion to serve his Brethren in
Masonry. The distillate of his mind and spirit has inspired confidence
in his work and has given to it enduring worth. His unfailing friendliness, charm o f manner, abundance of energy. eloquent rhetoric, and
keen sense of humor unite to form an inspiring disposition. He meets
the final test of a great leader, for he leaves behind him in other men
the conviction and will to carry on the prodigious work of Freemasonry.
He is every inch of him , in every fiber , a true Mason.
In the words of Shakespeare, he "Bear ( s) his blushing honours
thick upon him."

168

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

Prologue
"'" * *a still small voice."
- I KJNGSc.19,v.1 2.

The ritual of this august body prescribes that it is the duty of the
Grand Orator "to deliver at each annual communication an address to
the Grand Lodge upon matters appertaining to the Craft." The performance of this duty is a pleasant privilege and a high honor for me,
but it is with utmost humility that I discharge the task. The foregoing is
stated with deep sincerity, for a reading of the Grand Orations since the
establishment of this Grand Lodge in 1850 has impressed upon me the
clarity of thought and brilliance of expression by many erudite predecessors. I am comforted by one of the noteworthy precepts of our noble Fraternity; that when we are cloaked as Masons we meet on the same level
-where brotherly love prevails-and I know my Brethren are too charitable and too gracious not to accept my humble efforts in real Masonic
spirit. A Scottish cleric ( Nor man Macleod) truly said: " There's a star
to guide the humble .... *." I hope that I may not be considered too audacious in reaching for that star and in seeking to •invoke the blessing set
forth in the Book of our faith: "Blessed are the meek: for they shall
inherit the earth" (MATTHEW c. 5, v. 5; see also. PSALM 37, v. 11 ).
During past years, at occasions of this nature, there have been orations by Masons of great stature which may be classified as brilliant.
learned, lucid and scintillating. The Grand Orations during the existence
of this Grand Lodge disclose that in general they deal with the origin
and mysteries of our Order. the beauties of our ritual and our symbols,
the benign influence of the Masonic Order in the establishment of freedom
in this nation and elsewhere, the contribution of Freemasonry to public
welfare and the progress of human institutions, the moral force of our
Craft a nd its members in the development of human character and in the
dissemination of truth and justice. the motivation for the confidence of
true Masons in the Golden Rule. the obedience of Masons to the rule of
law, the belief of Masons in the dignity and rights of the individual. and
above all, the firm conviction of Masons in the brotherhood of man and
the fatherhood of God.
Such encomiums cast upon Freemasonry may be justly deserved and
inspirationa l; however, I am remindea of the saying of Ralph Waldo
Emerson that "What you do speaks so loud that I cannot hear what you
say." In short, we live in an age of technologica l marvels where scientific
accomplishmen ts, unbelievable a few years ago. demand impelling action.
Americans once again are battling for their very existence, but this time
on a world-wide battlefield. We are in a life-and-death struggle with

169

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

Communism. We are confronted with the supreme test of our spiritual.
moral. mental and physical strength. It is a test to determine whether
free men are fitted to govern themselves or whether a despot or insignificant minority shall direct the destinies of mankind. It is a conflict between
a tota lly materialistic philosophy and one which is based upon the principle that materialism must be guided and controlled by moral law. It is
not a new conflict; it extends back to the very beginning of human relations. But today the amazing technological and scientific achievements
have given man the power to destroy civilization and place the two
opposing ways of life in a real fight for survival. We must recognize that
we must meet our adversaries on all fronts where our free way of life is
challenged. We must recognize that, really, the cold war is a part of
World War III. This is the overriding problem of our generation and
of generations to follow.
This is a time when the proper and practical application of the
Masonic principles we all cherish may aid in the perpetuation of our
American way of life. This is a time when the spirit of Freemasonry
should be actuated in everyday life for the good and welfare of all of the
democratic human institutions without which our lives would be but a
desultory existence. We have truly reached "the times that try men's
souls."
Rather than again discuss the origin, history. philosphy, traditions or beauties of Freemasonry, it seems timely that pertinent phases
of this transcendent problem should be the subject of the Grand Oration
in the year 1960. It is not because of any lack of admiration or regard for
the history, philosophy and traditions of our beloved Fraternity, but because of an absolute trust in the principles of our Craft. that I seek to
encourage mature meditation and judicious reflection by this leading
group of Masons upon the real problem of our age-our survival as free
men.
There is precedent for such a practical approach in the peerless
Grand Oration of Past G rand Master Charles Albert Ada ms in 1910.
Fifty years ago, when he served this Grand Lodge 1s Grand Orator, he
delivered a sterling address on the subject, " Masonry in Business and
Politics." It is fitting and right that he should be honored at this Communication in recognition of his inspiring service in Masonry and also in
the community where he is so highly respected.

Another Sodom and Gomorrah?
"Where there is no vision, the people perish '" *
-

.. "

PROVERBS C. 29, V. 18.

Brethren! What if I were to tell you that this is your last d ay on
earth? What if I were to say that tomorrow the sky will open and nuclear

170

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GR AN D LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

bombs and missiles will rain down on your homes and families and veritably crush and destroy civilization? Unbelievable, you say? Perhaps so
fifteen years ago. But today, a decade and a half away from Hiroshima
and Nagasaki, even the most incredulous must acknowledge the dangers
that exist. For today it is an inescapable fact that almost half the human
race is now under despotic control; that the scientific knowledge of
nuclear fission is not possessed alone by the United States; and that
Communistic doctrine and tyrants pose an ever-present threat to the
peace and welfare of this nation as well as all the free people of the
world.

causes, there are seemingly reliable scientific explanations for the catastrophe. Dr. Werner Keller, in a recent book entitled The Bible A s History, apparently agrees with the American scholar Jack Finegan that
the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah probably took place about 1900
B. C. and that it "came about through a great earthquake which was
probably accompanied by explosions, lightning , issue of natural gas and
general conflagration."

For the skeptic or unbeliever, it is well to look to the events of the
past. The contemporary philosopher George Santayana said, "Those
who forget history are bound to repeat it." Let us not forget, but recall
to memory the account of the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah-a
narrative with a moral.
We read in the Holy Scriptures, in Chapter 18 of Genesis, that the
Lord came to Abraham and told him that he was going to destroy Sodom
and Gomorrah because they were such wicked cities. South of the Dead
Sea lay an extremely fertile plain, "the vale of Sodom, which is the salt
sea" (Gen., c. 14, v. 3). The Bible lists five towns in this valley-Sodom,
Gomorrah, Admah, Zeboiim, and Bela or Zoar (Gen. c. 14, v. 2), These
"cities of the plain" (Gen., c. 19, v. 29) were inhabited by people who
were corrupt, openly defying God and His law, and delighting in deeds
of violence. The profusion of wealth of the inhabitants of both Sodom
and Gomorrah gave birth to luxury and pride. The vilest and most brutal
passions were unrestrained and produced licentiousness ( Eze., c. 16, vv.
49-50). The fatal consequences of this were irreverence to God, inhospitality to strangers, and the indulgence in the most abominable vices.
These enormities highly offended the Almighty, who, in order to punish
the people, announced His vengeance both against them and against their
country. Persistent pleas by Abraham for the righteous in Sodom and
Gomorrah brought a final response from the Lord: "I will not destroy it
for ten's sake" (Gen., c. 18, v, 32). But there were not even ten righteous
people in all Sodom. "Then the Lord rained upon Sodom and upon
Gomorrah brimstone and fire from the Lord out of Heaven; And He
overthrew those cities, and all the plain. and all the inhabitants of the
cities, and that which grew upon the ground ... * * and lo, the smoke of
the country went up as the smoke of a furnace" (Gen., c. 19, vv. 24-28).
The story of Sodom and Gomorrah has been doubted, but extensive
exploration and archaeological research have disclosed evidence of
the trustworthiness of the Scriptures. Whether one believes the destruction resulted from divine action or was due to natural physical

171

The flames that consumed the cities of the plain shed their warning
light even down to our time. We are taught the fearful and solemn lesson
that, while God's mercy bears long with the transgressor. there is a limit
beyond which men must not go in sin. When tha t limit is reached , then
the offers of mercy are withdrawn and the ministration of judgment
begins. In all ages Sodom and Gomorrah have been synonymous w ith
immorality, wickedness and godlessness. The frightful disaster has made
a deep impression on men's minds and has served as a symbol of the
vengea nce of God for unrighteous living. The moral of the story is the
crowning virtue of righteousness.
Our American democracy is threatened not only by foreign ideologies
and vicious propaganda, but also by the unrighteous actions too frequently happening in private transactions and public life. America should
never come to the point where there should not be ten righteous men.
There should be always millions of honornble and unselfish men in th is
nation of abundance and freedom who are dedicated to the principles o f
equality under law; men who will nurture and sustain and strengthen our
American way of life. Yet the evident deterioration of public morality in
our land has caused acute and anguished apprehension among those who
realize that our strength and power as a free people come from respecting individual dignity, human rights and equal justice under law.
Our future survival has a basic dependence upon individual human
conduct. It poses for each American the question: How may I contribute
to the perpetuation of the American way of life. or indeed, our civilization? It presents to this audience of prominent Masons the question:
Have we a special task to perform in order to save our very lives and
humanity? An answer may be provided for each of you in what I call
The Spirit of Freemasonry in a Time That Tries Men's Souls-the subject of this Oration. That subject will be considered, albeit in the limited
time only briefly, to suggest salient factors, under four categories: first,
Freemasonry, Liberty and the Rule of Law; second, Freemasonry . T echnology and Public Education; third, Freemasonry. Politics, and the National Purpose; and, fourth, Freemasonry, Morality and Religion.
